Article Title: A 17-year-old North Carolina soldier killed in the Korean War and buried for decades as Unknown X-1642 is being laid to rest in Maryland, more than 70 years later, after DNA analysis finally identifie
Article Text:
Representative Image

Remains recovered but identity remained unknown

How scientists identified Boyd

A wider effort to identify the missing

Burial more than seven decades later

A US Army private who was killed during the Korean War at just 17 years old is finally being laid to rest under his own name, more than seven decades after his remains were buried as an unidentified soldier. Pvt. Joseph E. Boyd, from Bear Creek, North Carolina, was identified after forensic scientists analysed remains designated “Unknown X-1642”, according to the US Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA). The agency announced on October 17, 2026, that Boyd had been accounted for on June 10, with his burial scheduled for October 21 in Owings Mills, Maryland.Boyd was serving with Company A, 1st Battalion, 9th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, when he was reported missing on January 25, 1951, near Chigu-ri, South Korea. His disappearance occurred during patrol operations as US forces fought to clear enemy troops from mountainous areas near Wonju. His remains were not recovered at the time, leaving his fate unresolved for decades.In February 1951, a local villager discovered human remains near Saemal, South Korea. A US Army search-and-recovery team retrieved them and transferred them to the Central Identification Unit in Kokura, Japan, for examination.Despite the identification methods available at the time, investigators could not establish the person's identity.The remains were designated “Unknown X-1642 Tanggok” and, in 1956, were buried at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific in Honolulu, Hawaii. The cemetery, commonly known as the Punchbowl, became the final resting place for hundreds of unidentified American service members from the Korean War. Boyd's remains remained there for decades without his name being attached to them.The identification effort was part of a broader programme to resolve cases involving American service members whose remains had been recovered but could not be identified using the scientific techniques available at the time. In 2018, the DPAA proposed a plan to disinter 652 Korean War unknowns from the Punchbowl for renewed examination.As part of the programme, officials exhumed Unknown X-1642 in November 2023 and transferred the remains to a DPAA laboratory for further analysis. The renewed examination allowed specialists to compare the remains with records and evidence associated with service members who had been reported missing during the conflict.The identification relied on several forms of evidence rather than DNA testing alone. According to the DPAA, scientists combined dental and anthropological analysis with circumstantial evidence. Specialists from the Armed Forces Medical Examiner System also used mitochondrial DNA analysis and mitochondrial genome sequencing data to help establish the identity.The process illustrates how advances in forensic science can help resolve cases that remained uncertain for generations. Dental comparisons and anthropological examinations can help narrow the list of possible identities, while genetic analysis can provide additional evidence when suitable reference samples are available from relatives.The DPAA's wider disinterment programme involves researchers examining historical records, personnel files, unit documents and reports of earlier investigations alongside laboratory findings. Investigators compare the circumstances in which unidentified remains were recovered with the documented disappearance of missing service members. When the evidence indicates a likely match, the remains can be exhumed for detailed forensic analysis.Boyd's identification was announced after his family received a full briefing from officials, allowing the agency to release further details about the case.Boyd's case forms part of a continuing US effort to account for military personnel who went missing in past conflicts. According to the DPAA, more than 7,000 Americans remain unaccounted for from the Korean War, and the agency continues to investigate possible recovery sites and examine unidentified remains.The Korean War, fought from 1950 to 1953, left families across the United States without definitive answers about relatives who never returned. Some remains were recovered during or shortly after the fighting, but the methods available then were not always sufficient to identify them. Those remains were often buried as unknowns, with the possibility of future identification left open.The DPAA says its ongoing work combines historical research, field investigations and laboratory techniques, including DNA analysis, to provide families with answers where possible. The disinterment programme also allows officials to revisit remains that had previously been considered unidentifiable.Boyd's name had been recorded among the missing at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. Following his identification, the DPAA said a rosette would be placed next to his name at the Courts of the Missing to indicate that he had been accounted for. His burial was scheduled for October 21, 2026, in Owings Mills, Maryland.For a soldier who disappeared at 17, the identification brings an official resolution to a case that remained open for more than 75 years. The forensic work cannot recover the time his family spent without knowing what happened to him, but it has restored his identity to remains that had long been recorded only by a number.Boyd's case also demonstrates why the search for missing service members continues decades after a conflict ends. As forensic techniques improve and old records are revisited, remains once buried without names can sometimes be returned to families for burial with the recognition they were denied for generations.
Article Summary: Pvt. Joseph E. Boyd, from Bear Creek, North Carolina, was identified after forensic scientists analysed remains designated ‘Unknown X-1642’ The agency announced on October 17, 2026, that Boyd had been accounted for on June 10, with his burial scheduled for October 21 in Owings Mills, Maryland. Boyd was serving with Company A, 1st Battalion, 9th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, when he was reported missing on January 25, 1951, near Chigu-ri, South Korea.

Article Title: Meet Isabel Rossi, a Williamsburg, Virginia eighth-grader who tested a new way to position earthquake sensors; her mathematical model improved simulated coverage by 16.7% with just five additional dev
Article Text:
Isabel enjoys working through equations and mathematical proofs in her spare time (Photo: Society for science)

Importance of choosing sensor locations

Isabel enjoys working through equations and mathematical proofs in her spare time (Photo: Instagram/wjccschools)

What did the experiment find?

Isabel's love for mathematics

A 14-year-old student from Williamsburg, Virginia, has earned her a place among 30 finalists in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge for finding a new way to position earthquake sensors.Earthquake sensors can help detect seismic activity and provide early warnings, but deciding where to install them is not easy. Scientists must consider how accurately the devices can detect earthquakes, how much ground they can cover and whether their locations are accessible.According to The Virginian Pilot, Isabel Rossi, who carried out the research as an eighth-grader, developed a computer-based model that showed a possible 16.7% improvement in earthquake detection coverage using just five additional sensors.The finding emerged from a six-month project in which Isabel examined whether mathematical methods commonly used to make decisions could help identify better locations for earthquake sensors. For this, she worked with existing earthquake records and computer-generated sensor arrangements.Nearly 10,000 students applied to the national competition, which recognises research projects completed by middle school students across the United States.Isabel developed her project independently while attending James Blair Middle School. She is currently a freshman at Jamestown High School.According to Society for Science, which organises the challenge, Isabel's project, titled Listening in the Right Places: Game Theory and Optimisation for Earthquake Sensor Placement, was based on simulations.Earthquake monitoring depends on instruments that record seismic waves travelling through the ground. Some of these waves can be detected before stronger shaking reaches an area, allowing early warning systems to issue alerts. However, the usefulness of a sensor network also depends on where its instruments are located.For her study, Isabel concentrated on the Los Angeles region of California. She accessed a data library containing information about previous earthquakes and the locations of existing sensors. This allowed her to examine different arrangements without physically moving or installing any equipment.She wrote a computer program that generated random sets of possible sensor locations. Each arrangement was then assessed using two mathematical methods: a weighted sum model and Nash bargaining.The weighted sum model evaluates several objectives by assigning different levels of importance to them. Nash bargaining, a concept associated with game theory, looks for solutions that balance competing interests. Isabel used these approaches to examine the relationship between earthquake detection accuracy and sensor accessibility.The idea came after she read an article in Physics Today about the difficulties involved in detecting earthquakes. Having experienced a major earthquake herself, Isabel was already interested in the subject.Isabel compared their proposed sensor arrangements against the Pareto frontier, a mathematical concept used to identify solutions where improving one objective would mean making another worse.She examined whether an arrangement could provide better earthquake coverage without sacrificing another consideration, such as accessibility.Nash bargaining performed better in this comparison, producing arrangements closer to the Pareto frontier. Also, one model indicated that adding five sensors could improve simulated coverage by 16.7%.The finding does not establish that the same improvement would occur in an operational earthquake monitoring network. It does, however, show how mathematical modelling could help researchers compare possible sensor locations before making installation decisions.Isabel believes such methods could be particularly useful in places where reaching sensor locations is difficult or resources are limited.Isabel enjoys working through equations and mathematical proofs in her spare time and has described the precision of mathematics as one of its main attractions.“I like the precision of it. Over time it’s become one of my favorite free time activities," she told Society for Science.Her interest in scientific experiments began during childhood. Her father, Enrico Rossi, teaches physics at William & Mary, while her mother, Margarita Marinova, is an English professor at Christopher Newport University. Isabel also grew up watching her older sister Eleanor use chemistry and physics experiment sets.At nine, she began meeting a retired NASA engineer introduced to her by a teacher. Their activities included building homemade rockets, measuring their launches and making adjustments to improve their performance.She later organised a MathCounts team at James Blair Middle School and helped arrange a STEAM event to encourage younger students to explore science and mathematics. She continues to coach the mathematics team.Isabel also plays violin in the Williamsburg Youth Orchestra and participates in environmental science activities. She has expressed interest in careers involving aerospace engineering, applied mathematics or medicine.The national competition's final round will take place in Washington, DC, from October 23 to 28, bringing together students from 17 states and Puerto Rico. Finalists will compete for more than $100,000 in awards, including a $25,000 grand prize.
Article Summary: Isabel Rossi is among 30 finalists in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge for finding a new way to position earthquake sensors. She developed a computer-based model that showed a possible 16.7% improvement in earthquake detection coverage using just five additional sensors. Nearly 10,000 students applied to the national competition, which recognises research projects completed by middle school students across the United States.

Article Title: California has created its first new marine protected areas in over a decade, adding about 15,000 acres of safeguarded coastal waters, including kelp habitats off Malibu and tribal-nominated sites nea
Article Text:
California strengthened Pyramid Point protections to aid declining fish populations while preserving tribal harvesting rights.

A new chapter for marine protection

Tribal stewardship takes centre stage

Conservation meets economic concerns

Protecting a changing coastline

Along California’s vast coastline, some of the ocean’s most valuable real estate now has a new layer of protection. From kelp forests off Malibu to biologically rich waters near Santa Barbara and Point Sal, the state has expanded its marine conservation network for the first time in more than a decade, adding roughly 15,000 acres of safeguarded coastal waters.The move comes at a consequential moment for California’s coastline, as debates over fishing access, tribal stewardship, climate change and potential offshore oil development intensify, states the latest report by Santa Monica Daily Press (SMDP).According to the SMDP, the California Fish and Game Commission approved the latest changes following a three-year process involving tribes, fishermen, scientists, local governments and members of the public. The additions bring approximately 22.2% of California’s coastal waters under conservation, moving the state closer to its target of protecting 30% of its waters by 2030.One of the most significant changes expands the Point Dume State Marine Conservation Area off Malibu. The extension encompasses additional kelp forest habitat, an ecosystem increasingly important as warming ocean conditions place pressure on marine life.The state has also established two new conservation areas: the Point Sal State Marine Conservation Area in San Luis Obispo County and the Mishopshno State Marine Conservation Area near Carpinteria in Santa Barbara County.The new areas mark a historic development for California’s marine protection network because they are the first sites in the system to emerge from tribal nominations.The Point Sal proposal was co-led by the Northern Chumash Tribal Council, while the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians helped champion the Mishopshno designation. Both areas hold ecological as well as cultural significance, strengthening the possibility of greater collaboration between tribal communities and state agencies.The Los Angeles Times reported that Point Sal encompasses kelp forests, Lion Rock and habitats used by sea lions, seals and migratory birds. The waters near Carpinteria Reef, meanwhile, include one of the Santa Barbara Channel’s healthiest kelp forests, alongside important nursery habitat for marine species.The Mishopshno area takes its name from a nearby historic Chumash village, reflecting the connection between cultural heritage and marine conservation.The new protections have not been welcomed universally. While environmental groups and conservation advocates have celebrated the designations, commercial and recreational fishermen have raised concerns about losing access to productive fishing grounds.Under the new rules, both tribal-nominated conservation areas allow hook-and-line fishing from shore but prohibit commercial fishing and boat-based recreational fishing within their boundaries.For fishing businesses, that could mean longer journeys to reach accessible waters, potentially increasing costs and reducing opportunities for affordable family fishing trips. Commercial fishermen have also questioned whether the environmental benefits have been weighed against the potential economic and social consequences.The California Department of Fish and Wildlife had advised against creating the new protected areas, recommending that tribal management opportunities be explored through a separate process. The Ocean Protection Council, however, supported the designations.The latest additions are part of a broader reassessment of California’s marine protected area network, which was completed in 2012. State monitoring has found that protected waters can support marine biodiversity while creating benefits for surrounding fisheries and coastal tourism.The timing is particularly significant as California faces growing pressure from climate change and renewed federal interest in offshore oil and gas leasing.The state has also strengthened protections at Pyramid Point on the North Coast, aiming to help declining fish populations while continuing tribal harvest of a culturally important species, states The LA Times report.For conservation advocates, the expanded network represents more than a collection of protected zones. Connecting habitats can help marine ecosystems become more resilient as ocean temperatures rise and environmental pressures increase, adds SMDP report.California still has ground to cover before reaching its 30% marine conservation goal. But after more than a decade without new state marine protected areas, the latest designations signal a renewed effort to treat the coastline not simply as a resource to be used, but as an ecosystem worth preserving for generations to come.Images Courtesy: istock
Article Summary: The state has expanded its marine conservation network for the first time in more than a decade, adding roughly 15,000 acres of safeguarded coastal waters. The additions bring approximately 22.2% of California’s coastal waters under conservation, moving the state closer to its target of protecting 30% of its waters by 2030. The move comes as debates over fishing access, tribal stewardship, climate change and potential offshore oil development intensify.

Article Title: Since 1987, an 86-year-old Texas man named Dale has spent decades building a 62-foot boat in his yard; when three visitors discovered his dream, strangers helped raise money to finish and move it
Article Text:
How three visitors discovered Dale's dream

Crowdfunding effort aims to get the boat into the water

A dream nearly four decades in the making

An 86-year-old Texas man has spent nearly four decades building a 62-foot steel boat in his front yard, hoping to one day sail it to Alaska. Now, after three visitors discovered his long-standing dream, strangers have come together to help him finish the vessel and move it to a launch site. According to a report by Good News Network, Dale, a resident of Mineral Wells, Texas, began the project in 1987, and his boat is now approximately 75% complete.The vessel features four staterooms, a master bedroom, a lounge, a kitchen and an engine room. However, completing the ambitious project has become increasingly difficult, and moving the massive steel structure out of his yard will require heavy machinery. With the boat still waiting to reach the water, an unexpected encounter has given Dale's decades-long dream fresh momentum.The story took an unexpected turn when three Englishmen, Laurence Benson, Benjie and Will, who were working in Texas, learned about Dale's boat through their friend Kiah. Kiah, who was in the area for work, spotted the unusual vessel and sent Laurence a video, encouraging him to meet its builder.In the GoFundMe campaign he launched to help Dale, Laurence described how the group travelled from Fort Worth to meet him."We tried calling, but couldn’t get through. So we drove an hour and a half from Fort Worth and turned up unannounced. Benjie knocked on the door and spoke to Dale’s wife. Dale was still putting his socks on," Laurence wrote.The visitors soon discovered that the boat was much more than an unfinished construction project. As Dale began talking about it, his enthusiasm for the vessel and his ambition to sail it to Alaska became apparent. Laurence said Dale even climbed a ladder to show the visitors the deck, despite reportedly not having been up there for years.The encounter was recorded and shared on Instagram, where the video attracted around 670,000 likes and more than 6,000 comments, bringing Dale's story to a much wider audience.Moved by Dale's determination, Laurence and his friends decided to help him take the next step towards completing the vessel. They launched a fundraising campaign to cover the remaining construction work, the equipment needed to bring the boat down the hill from the yard and its transportation to a suitable launch site.According to the campaign, the boat's size and location make moving it a significant logistical challenge. Even after years of welding and construction, getting the vessel onto the water requires more than finishing its remaining components.Within days, the campaign raised more than $41,000 towards its $45,000 target, with contributions from more than 1,500 donors, according to the reported figures. Laurence estimated that approximately $50,000 would be needed to move the boat and get it into the water.The fundraising effort, however, is not intended to end with the vessel's relocation. Laurence has said he wants to work with Dale's family to help see the project through to completion and give the boatbuilder a chance to fulfil his lifelong ambition.Dale's project has taken shape over a period when much of the world around him has changed. What began in his front yard in 1987 has grown into a 62-foot vessel, built piece by piece over the years. While the boat is not yet ready to sail, the response to his story has demonstrated how a personal dream can bring together people who have never met its owner.For Dale, the immediate challenge is to complete the remaining work and get the boat safely to a launch site. Whether the vessel will ultimately make the journey to Alaska remains to be seen, but the support from strangers has brought him closer to a goal he has pursued for nearly 40 years.
Article Summary: Dale, a resident of Mineral Wells, Texas, began the project in 1987. The vessel features four staterooms, a master bedroom, a lounge, a kitchen and an engine room. Three Englishmen, Laurence Benson, Benjie and Will, who were working in Texas, learned about Dale's boat through their friend Kiah. The group travelled from Fort Worth to meet him.

Article Title: A California geologist spotted a strange object sticking out of a creek; a Google reverse image search suggested it was an Ice Age mastodon tooth at least 10,000 years old
Article Text:
The fossilised mastodon molar protruding from a creek bed in a Midpen preserve in California.

A reverse image search pointed to the identification

The tooth is at least 10,000 years old, and may be much older

Stanford will keep and scan the fossil

The discovery site will remain undisclosed

A California geomorphologist surveying a creek for a habitat restoration project noticed an unusual object lying half in and half out of the water. Unsure what she had found, she turned to Google’s reverse image search for clues. The search suggested it might be a molar from an Ice Age mastodon, and a paleontologist later confirmed it. The tooth belonged to an ancient Pacific mastodon, a mammal that roamed North America thousands of years ago. It was found in a Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen) preserve in San Mateo County, during work to improve habitat for threatened California red-legged frogs. Researchers are now working to establish its age and significance.Brigid Lynch, a geomorphologist with Balance Hydrologics, found the object while conducting field surveys for the habitat enhancement project. When a reverse image search suggested it could be a mastodon molar, Midpen and her team contacted paleontologists for confirmation.Wayne Thompson, a paleontologist with Pacific Paleontology, confirmed it as an upper left molar from a Pacific mastodon (Mammut pacificus).The tooth measures about 8.5 inches long, 7 inches deep and 3 inches wide, and it retains both its crown and roots.Thompson called it “the most complete mastodon molar from our area” and the most spectacular he has ever seen. Mastodon teeth are often found broken, which makes the condition of this one especially significant.The tooth is estimated to be at least 10,000 years old, but its precise age has not been established. Thompson told Fox News Digital it could be between 50,000 and 100,000 years old. Researchers at Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability plan to analyze the tooth to learn more about its age, the animal’s diet and its environment.Pacific mastodons were large herbivores that lived in western North America during the Pleistocene epoch, which ended about 11,700 years ago. Although related to modern elephants, they differed from mammoths in several ways, including their teeth and feeding habits. Mastodons primarily browsed on leaves, shoots and other vegetation rather than grazing mainly on grasses.Pacific mastodons were identified as a species distinct from the American mastodon in 2019, following extensive study of mastodon bones found in Southern California.Midpen donated the fossil to Stanford University to support further scientific study. Stanford will also produce a 3D scan of the tooth for Midpen to use in educational outreach, which allows people to examine the specimen without handling the original.The fossil could help scientists understand the animals that once inhabited the Bay Area and the ecosystems in which they lived. Such discoveries provide clues about past biodiversity and environmental change.Midpen is not revealing the exact location, so that visitors do not go looking for their own fossils. Thompson has said the tooth may have recently separated from a skull that remains buried at the site, though this has not been confirmed.The find also offers an unexpected link between ancient wildlife and modern conservation. Lynch came across the fossil while working on a project to improve habitat for the threatened California red-legged frog. A survey meant to support a species facing present-day pressures instead uncovered evidence of an animal that disappeared thousands of years ago.
Article Summary: The tooth belonged to an ancient Pacific mastodon, a mammal that roamed North America thousands of years ago. It was found in a preserve in San Mateo County, California, during work to improve habitat for threatened California red-legged frogs. Researchers are now working to establish its age and significance.

Article Title: In 2022, researchers began monitoring oyster habitat restoration beneath China's Bohai Bay; by 2026, artificial reefs held 286 oysters per square metre and suspended particles were about 62% lower
Article Text:
How the oyster reefs were restored

Oyster numbers increased over time

Other marine animals also began returning

Why more monitoring is needed

Four years after researchers began studying the restoration of oyster reefs in China's Bohai Bay, the newly created habitats are showing signs of recovery. A survey conducted in March 2026 found an average of 286 oysters per square metre on artificial reefs. The amount of suspended material in the surrounding water was also about 62% lower than it had been before the restoration work began.The findings come from a study by Chang Liu and fellow researchers, published in Frontiers in Marine Science . Their work followed changes in marine life and water conditions at Dashentang, near Tianjin, from 2022 to 2026.The reduction in suspended particles was among the changes recorded during this period. In May 2022, researchers measured an average of 19.3 milligrams of suspended particulate matter per litre of water. When they returned in March 2026, the figure was 7.28 milligrams per litre. Suspended particulate matter includes fine sediment and other small particles carried in the water.Although oysters can remove particles from water as they feed, the study does not establish that they caused this decline. The researchers did not directly measure the oysters' filtration activity, and changes in the surrounding environment may also have affected water conditions.Dashentang once had a much larger natural oyster habitat. During the 1970s, its reefs covered around 35 square kilometres. In recent years, that area had fallen to just 1.69 square kilometres.According to Devdiscourse, fishing activities, shoreline development and changing seabed conditions were among the factors behind the decline. The problem is not limited to China, with the study citing estimates that approximately 85% of oyster reefs worldwide have been lost.Restoring the habitat is not easy as the reefs remain underwater, at depths of around two to five metres. Fine sediment on the seabed can also be moved by currents and cover the surfaces needed by young oysters to settle and grow.The restoration work, carried out between August 2022 and December 2023, involved placing 4,500 reinforced-concrete structures and 41,250 oyster-shell frames in the area. The aim was to provide surfaces where oysters could attach themselves while also creating habitat for other marine animals. The installed structures had a combined volume of 345,000 cubic metres.The first surveys showed that oyster populations on the artificial structures were still small. In November 2023, while construction was under way, researchers recorded an average of 65 oysters per square metre.There was little improvement at first. The average fell to 58.8 in March 2024 before increasing to 86.6 in June that year. A much larger rise was recorded in March 2026, when the figure reached 286 oysters per square metre.The existing natural reefs supported considerably more oysters. Their average density had been around 80 per square metre before restoration, but increased sharply during the construction period. By March 2026, researchers counted an average of 1,830.4 oysters per square metre on natural reefs.Another finding concerned the arrival of young oysters. Scientists refer to this process as recruitment, which helps indicate whether new oysters are joining a population.In March 2026, artificial reefs had an average of 204.2 young oysters per square metre measuring less than 20 millimetres. Most oysters on these structures were still small or medium-sized, suggesting that the populations had not yet fully developed.The researchers did not limit their observations to oysters. They also counted macrobenthos, a term used for animals such as clams, worms and crustaceans that live on or within the seabed.These animals initially became less numerous. Before restoration, the study recorded an average of 140.5 individuals per square metre. During construction, that number dropped to 30.4. By March 2026, however, the average had reached 255.6.The change was particularly noticeable on artificial reefs. In March 2024, these areas supported 29.4 seabed animals per square metre. Two years later, the number had risen to 405.2.It was not just the number of animals that changed. Before restoration, molluscs made up 98.1% of the recorded seabed community. Their share decreased during the early stages of recovery and stood at 66.3% in March 2026.Worms and arthropods accounted for a greater share than before. According to the researchers, the developing reef structures provided different places for marine animals to live, find shelter and feed.The team also examined dissolved oxygen, which marine organisms need to survive. Its concentration had fallen during construction and the early restoration period, but reached 7.87 milligrams per litre by March 2026, close to the level measured before restoration. Meanwhile, Nitrogen concentrations and chlorophyll-a varied during the monitoring period.The findings point to an increase in marine life at Dashentang, but the researchers stopped short of attributing every change to the restoration work.The study was based on five surveys conducted in different seasons between 2022 and 2026. Some sampling locations also changed during that time. Importantly, there were no separate comparison sites outside the restoration area that could help establish what might have happened without the project.Several questions therefore remain unanswered. The researchers did not directly measure how much material the oysters filtered from the water, how much nutrient removal occurred or whether sediment was accumulating around the structures. They also did not assess whether the artificial reefs were sinking.The team recommended further monitoring of young oyster survival, sediment build-up and the stability of the structures. While the March 2026 findings show that oyster populations and other seabed animals have increased, it is still too early to determine whether the restored reefs can sustain themselves over the long term.
Article Summary: Oyster reefs in China's Bohai Bay are showing signs of recovery. A survey conducted in March 2026 found an average of 286 oysters per square metre on artificial reefs. The amount of suspended material in the surrounding water was also about 62% lower than it had been before the restoration work began.

Article Title: Mariska Hargitay helped fund Detroit’s effort to test abandoned sexual assault kits; by April 2025, the wider project had secured 263 convictions as investigations continued across decades
Article Text:
Hargitay also helped draw attention to the issue among lawmakers (AP file photo)

How Hargitay became involved in the investigation

Why testing the evidence took years

Cases reached far beyond Detroit

Investigations continue despite completion of testing

More than 250 convictions have emerged from a long-running investigation into thousands of sexual assault cases in Detroit, Michigan, where evidence had remained untested for decades. American actress Mariska Hargitay , best known for her role as detective Olivia Benson in Law & Order: SVU, was among those who helped fund and support the effort. According to the Wayne County Prosecutor's Office, the Detroit Sexual Assault Kit Project had secured 263 convictions by April 2025, while investigations and prosecutions were still continuing.The project began in 2009, when authorities discovered 11,341 sexual assault evidence kits inside a Detroit Police Department warehouse. According toAccording to Wayne County, Michigan, the kits related to cases dating from 1984 to 2009, but none had been submitted for testing. The discovery meant that evidence collected over 25 years was still awaiting examination.Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy took responsibility for addressing the backlog. However, examining such a large number of kits required considerable funding, which was difficult to secure at the time. Detroit was facing serious financial problems, and the county administration did not initially provide the money needed for the project.Worthy began approaching organisations and private donors for assistance. What followed was a fundraising effort involving government agencies, charitable foundations and individuals from across the United States and abroad. Hargitay's Joyful Heart Foundation eventually became one of the organisations supporting the initiative.Hargitay had already been working with survivors of sexual assault through the Joyful Heart Foundation when she met Worthy at a congressional hearing in 2010. Their meeting marked the beginning of the foundation's involvement in Detroit's effort to examine the abandoned evidence.Her contribution was not limited to financial support. Hargitay also helped draw attention to the issue among lawmakers, using her public profile to support Worthy's campaign for changes in the handling of sexual assault evidence.In a 2024 interview featured on the Dateline: True Crime Weekly podcast, Worthy recalled asking Hargitay to come to Detroit after they had appeared before lawmakers. "She said she would, and she did," Worthy said.The actress subsequently attended a breakfast organised for legislators whom Worthy had struggled to reach. According to the prosecutor, Hargitay's presence helped bring attention to the issue and encouraged political support for reforms. "And I am telling you, that legislation that helped us crack this problem in Michigan sailed through," Worthy recalled.One of the biggest challenges was the cost of examining the evidence. According to the Los Angeles Times, which reported on the podcast in August 2024, testing a single kit could cost between $1,200 and $1,500. With 11,341 kits awaiting examination, the authorities needed millions of dollars.Funding eventually came from several sources, including the federal government, Michigan authorities, Wayne County and private organisations. Donations were also received from people in all 50 US states and nine foreign countries.The work went beyond examining evidence already held by police. Investigators also had to follow up on findings from cases that were sometimes decades old.The results showed how serious the consequences of leaving evidence untested could be. In one case highlighted by the Wayne County Prosecutor's Office, evidence from a 2002 sexual assault was linked to a man who had later been imprisoned for three murders committed during the following seven years.By the project's tenth anniversary in 2019, according to the prosecutor's office, testing of all 11,341 kits had been completed.The investigation eventually extended well beyond Michigan. By April 2025, cases connected to the Detroit project had been linked to 40 US states, including California, Texas, New York, Florida and Washington.The Los Angeles Times reported that the effort had helped solve more than 5,000 cases and identify 22 serial rapists, citing information shared through NBC's coverage of the project.The work also contributed to changes in how Michigan handles sexual assault evidence. The state introduced legislation establishing timelines for submitting kits for testing, along with a tracking system that allows survivors to follow the progress of DNA testing.Hargitay later helped bring the issue to television audiences through I Am Evidence, a 2018 documentary she produced. The film examined the problem of untested sexual assault kits and featured Worthy's efforts in Detroit. It received an Emmy Award in 2019.Although the original kits have been tested, the cases connected to them have not all reached a conclusion. The Wayne County Prosecutor's Office said investigations and prosecutions were continuing in 2025, more than 15 years after the evidence was discovered.Worthy has remained associated with Hargitay's foundation, serving as its vice-chair and co-chair of its National Council of Leadership and Innovation.The Detroit project has also been used to develop practices for investigating sexual assault cases and managing evidence in other parts of the United States.
Article Summary: Mariska Hargitay helped fund and support the Detroit Sexual Assault Kit Project. The project began in 2009, when authorities discovered 11,341 evidence kits. The kits related to cases dating from 1984 to 2009, but none had been submitted for testing. The discovery meant evidence collected over 25 years was still awaiting examination.

Article Title: Kim Jong Un photos released to dismiss rumours of coma, takeover by sister
Article Text:
Kim Jong Un inspects pink shoe, women’s coats as death rumours grip North Korea

How the death rumours began

Claims of Chinese troop deployment

What is known about Kim's health?

North Korean supreme leader Kim Jong Un has resurfaced in photographs released by state media, inspecting children's footwear and women's clothing, after unverified claims circulated online that he had died from a brain haemorrhage.The photographs, published by North Korea's official media on Monday, show Kim examining footwear, gesturing towards officials and inspecting coats at a garment and footwear exhibition. The images emerged amid a wave of social media speculation about the 42-year-old leader's health and the possibility of a succession crisis in the secretive country, the New York Post reported.According to North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency, Kim toured the exhibition on Monday. However, the photographs have not been independently authenticated, and it remains unclear precisely when they were taken.One image shows Kim bending forward to inspect a small pink shoe held by a woman. In another, he gestures with his arms outstretched as he appears to address an official. A third photograph captures him reaching towards the sleeve of a woman's coat displayed on a mannequin.The speculation gathered pace after Wanjun Xie, a US-based Chinese dissident associated with the China Democracy Party, posted a series of claims on X alleging that Kim had died and that his sister, Kim Yo Jong , had taken control of the country.In a post on Monday, Xie wrote: "Rumours of the death of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un have been circulating online for days, but Kim Jong Un has not yet made a public appearance to deny them. This indirectly confirms that the rumours of Kim Jong Un's death are likely true. Furthermore, it is rumoured that after Kim Jong-un's death, the North Korean regime has not been transferred to his daughter Kim Ju-ae, but is currently in the hands of his sister Kim Yo-jong."After assuming power, Kim Yo-jong immediately activated loudspeaker broadcasts to South Korea and fired 201 warning shots. She also warned South Korea that North Korea was considering a comprehensive upgrade of its tactical strike capabilities. This sudden intensification of threats against South Korea is clearly aimed at strengthening her control over the North Korean military and consolidating her power through strong external threats. This indirectly confirms the rumors that Kim Jong-un is dead and that Kim Yo-jong is currently in control of the regime; these rumors are likely true."The New York Post reported that Xie's claims began gaining traction on Sunday. However, the allegations have not been supported by medical records, identifiable witnesses or other independently verifiable evidence.In another post on Sunday, Xie claimed that Kim had suffered a severe cerebral haemorrhage, fallen into a coma and been transferred to Beijing for emergency treatment. He alleged that a team of specialists from Peking Union Medical College Hospital had travelled to North Korea before Kim was moved to China."It is rumoured that recently, Kim Jong-un, General Secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea and Supreme Leader of North Korea, suffered a severe cerebral haemorrhage and fell into a coma. Although a team of medical experts from Peking Union Medical College Hospital was dispatched to North Korea to assist in his treatment, the poor medical conditions in North Korea forced Kim Jong-un to be transferred to Peking Union Medical College Hospital for emergency treatment. However, due to the severity of his condition and the fact that the optimal window for treatment had passed, Kim Jong-un succumbed to his injuries and died. His body has been secretly transported back to North Korea, and the news of his death is being kept under wraps."Xie further alleged that Kim's body had been secretly returned to North Korea and that authorities were concealing news of his death. He also claimed that Chinese troops had been deployed to Pyongyang amid fears of a succession crisis.In a separate post, he wrote: "It is said that on October 17, Peking Union Medical College Hospital dispatched a team of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular medical experts to North Korea to participate in the rescue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who was in critical condition."Xie's posts also fuelled speculation about a possible power struggle involving Kim's daughter, Kim Ju-ae, and his sister, Kim Yo Jong. He claimed that China had sent 9,000 troops to Pyongyang to help stabilise the situation.The claims of Kim's death, a Chinese troop deployment and a possible succession crisis remain unverified. North Korean authorities have not explicitly addressed the death reports.Kim's health has long been the subject of international speculation. The New York Post reported that South Korea's National Intelligence Service told lawmakers on September 30 that Kim weighed approximately 140 kilograms (309 pounds) and faced an elevated risk of cardiovascular disease because of severe obesity.However, the agency reportedly detected no significant signs of ill health, pointing to Kim's ability to run up stairs during an inspection of a naval destroyer.The latest rumours echo a false alarm in 2020, when Ji Seong-ho, a North Korean defector who later became a South Korean lawmaker, claimed he was "99%" certain that Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Kim subsequently appeared in public, and Ji apologised for making the erroneous claim.The New York Post said it had sought comment from the governments of North Korea and China, as well as Peking Union Medical College Hospital.
Article Summary: North Korean supreme leader Kim Jong Un has resurfaced in photographs released by state media. The images emerged amid a wave of social media speculation about the 42-year-old leader's health and the possibility of a succession crisis. Unverified claims circulated online that he had died from a brain haemorrhage.

Article Title: Typhoon Champi: Taiwan issues land warning, cancels 125 flights as powerful storm approaches
Article Text:
Nasa's Terra satellite shows Typhoon Noul in the Pacific Ocean, approaching Taiwan and Japan's main islands on its northward journey (Reuters image)

Taiwan issued a land warning for powerful Typhoon Champi on Thursday and cancelled 125 flights as the storm approached the island's northeastern coast, bringing the threat of destructive winds, torrential rain and waves exceeding six metres, Reuters reported.Champi, which was previously classified as a super typhoon, weakened slightly but continued to pack gusts of more than 227 kmph near its centre, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration. The storm was about 520 km southeast of Taiwan's southern tip and was expected to pass close to the northeastern coast late on Friday before moving north towards the Chinese coast.Taiwan President Lai Ching-te urged residents to prepare for the storm and avoid mountainous and coastal areas."A little more preparation means less risk," he wrote on his Facebook page.Mobile phone alerts warning of waves exceeding six metres were issued to coastal towns, while rainfall approaching one metre was forecast in northern mountainous areas, including hills near the capital Taipei. Weather experts warned that the storm's impact could last nearly two days.Taiwan's transport ministry said 125 flights had been cancelled on Thursday, mostly domestic services, while the rail network remained unaffected.The interior ministry said no evacuations had been reported.Champi is also forecast to pass over Yonaguni, Japan's westernmost inhabited island in Okinawa Prefecture. Japan Airlines, ANA and Skymark cancelled more than 100 flights between Thursday and Sunday, mostly domestic services, disrupting travel for more than 11,000 passengers.
Article Summary: Taiwan issues land warning for powerful Typhoon Champi. 125 flights cancelled as storm approaches island's northeastern coast. Threat of destructive winds, torrential rain and waves exceeding six metres. Japan Airlines, ANA and Skymark cancel more than 100 flights between Thursday and Sunday.

Article Title: Explosion, fuel leak: Two Syrian pipelines damaged in fresh blow to war-hit energy network
Article Text:
Security forces of Syria's Interior Ministry guard the al-Omar oil field, the country's largest by area and production

Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday, with one explosion triggering a fire and another causing a fuel leak, Syrian state media reported.According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), citing the state-owned Syrian Petroleum Company, an explosion struck the Jbessa gas pipeline in Hasakah province, while a separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.The explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze.The Syrian Petroleum Company described the incident as sabotage. Officials said alternative arrangements would maintain gas supplies to power stations during repairs, while domestic gas supplies remained unaffected.In a separate incident, a hole was discovered in the Baniyas-Homs pipeline in the Hadida area west of Homs, causing a leak of petroleum products. Emergency and technical teams were deployed to contain the leak and isolate the damaged section.Al Jazeera, citing Syrian state media, reported that the damage to the Baniyas-Homs pipeline was believed to be linked to an attempted fuel theft. The initial reports did not confirm the cause or identify those responsible.The incidents come amid a series of disruptions to Syria’s energy infrastructure. Earlier in October, an oil pipeline near Tal Hamis in Hasakah province was damaged in what the Syrian Petroleum Company described as sabotage.Syria is working to rebuild its oil and gas infrastructure after years of conflict, restoring production in northeastern oilfields and reconnecting them with processing facilities and refineries in Homs and Baniyas.In January 2026, the Syrian Petroleum Company began pumping raw gas from the Jbessa fields in Hasakah to the Furqlus gas plant in Homs countryside at around 1.2 million cubic metres per day to support electricity generation.The second damaged pipeline, connecting Baniyas on the Mediterranean coast to Homs, transports petroleum products between two important energy centres. The Baniyas refinery is undergoing an overhaul aimed at increasing its processing capacity from around 80,000 to 130,000 barrels per day.Syria has also undertaken emergency pipeline repairs and plans to expand its transportation network. A September 2026 analysis by the Baker Institute for Public Policy reported that the Syrian Petroleum Company was repairing existing infrastructure and planning a heavy-crude pipeline linking northeastern oilfields to the Baniyas refinery.
Article Summary: Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday. One explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze. A separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.

Article Title: Kylie Jenner launched a lip kit in 2015 and built a global cosmetics brand; Coty agreed to pay $600 million for a 51% stake in 2019
Article Text:
Image: Left/Britannica/Right/Refinery29

How the November 2015 Kylie Lip Kit launch became Kylie Cosmetics, a beauty brand with global reach

Kylie Cosmetics stand at Melbourne Airport, Australia. Image Credit: Wikipedia

Why Coty agreed to pay 600 million dollars for 51 per cent ownership of the Kylie Jenner partnership

Kylie Jenner arrives at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party on Sunday, March 15, 2026, at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art in LA.

177 million dollars in revenue, growth targets and the financial case for Coty

How creative control, licensing and Coty's manufacturing reach shaped the global beauty expansion plan

Where Coty stands today as a global beauty company and how the Kylie Jenner partnership fits its plans

Few beauty stories capture the power of social media as clearly as the rise of Kylie Jenner 's cosmetics business. What began in November 2015 as a debut lip kit became Kylie Cosmetics, a brand that built a devoted audience online and then attracted one of the largest beauty companies in the world. In November 2019, that company, Coty, agreed to buy a majority stake in the business for 600 million dollars. Here’s how the brand grew, what the agreement contained, why the numbers mattered, and how the partnership was designed to carry the business into new global markets. The deal also marked a turning point in the influencer-led beauty industry, demonstrating how a strong digital following could translate into a valuable global consumer brand.Coty's press release describes the origin story plainly. In November 2015, Kylie Jenner launched Kylie Cosmetics, and the debut product, the Kylie Lip Kit, was a sell-out success. Her online store, KylieCosmetics.com, is one of the most successful online stores in the world, and the range grew well beyond lips to include eyeliners, eyeshadows, blushes, highlighters, concealers, brushes and makeup bags, plus limited edition sets released throughout the year.In May 2019, she introduced Kylie Skin, a range of skincare products. The audience behind it was enormous, Coty says she has more than 270 million followers across her personal and brand social media channels, and that both brands are among the fastest-growing and most-engaged beauty brands on social media. Forbes featured her as the youngest-ever self-made billionaire in August 2018.On 18 November 2019, Coty and Kylie Jenner announced a long-term strategic partnership. Under the terms of the agreement, Coty would acquire 51 per cent ownership in the partnership for 600 million dollars, and the acquisition was expected to close in the third quarter of Coty's fiscal year 2020. Coty described the transaction as a key milestone in its ongoing transformation into a more focused and agile company. Chairman of the Board Peter Harf told the public that the partnership was an exciting step in Coty's renewed emphasis on its beauty business, calling Kylie Jenner a modern-day icon with an incredible sense of the beauty consumer. Pierre Laubies, Coty's chief executive officer, told the public the company was pleased to welcome her into its organisation and family.Coty's press release sets out the financial case in specific terms. Kylie Cosmetics generated an estimated 177 million dollars in net revenues over the preceding twelve months. Coty said it expected the transaction to add more than 1 per cent per year to the net revenue growth of its core fragrance, cosmetics and skin care portfolio over the next three years. The company also expected the deal to be neutral to its earnings per share in the first year and to add to them afterwards, and it expected the return on invested capital to exceed its cost of capital by fiscal year 2023. Tiger Shark served as an advisor to Coty on the transaction. Coty also scheduled a conference call that morning, with the live audio webcast and presentation slides made available through its investor relations website.The agreement divides responsibilities along each side's strengths. Together, Coty and Kylie Jenner set and lead the strategic direction, focusing on global expansion and entry into new beauty categories. Kylie Jenner and her team keep leading all creative efforts in product and communications, building on her global reach through social media. Coty takes overall responsibility for developing the portfolio, drawing on its knowledge of research and development, manufacturing, distribution and commercial strategy, and it acts as licensee for skincare, fragrances and nail products. All beauty categories continue to be sold through leading luxury beauty retailers and owned digital channels. Both parties aim to build what Coty calls a high-growth, digitally native beauty brand. Kylie Jenner told the public the partnership lets her team stay focused on creating and developing each product while building an international beauty powerhouse.Coty's own investor relations website shows the scale of the company that Kylie Jenner partnered with. Founded in Paris in 1904, Coty describes itself as one of the world's largest beauty companies, with a portfolio spanning fragrance, colour cosmetics, and skin and body care. The site lists the company as second globally in both fragrances and mass colour cosmetics, with more than 60 brands and licenses, about 11,300 employees, seven manufacturing sites and sales in more than 120 countries. For fiscal 2026, it reports net revenues of 5.8 billion dollars, adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of 847 million dollars, and free cash flow of 348 million dollars. Pairing that infrastructure with a creator-led brand is what the partnership set out to do.
Article Summary: Coty and Kylie Jenner announced a long-term strategic partnership. Under the terms of the agreement, Coty would acquire 51 per cent ownership in the partnership for 600 million dollars. The acquisition was expected to close in the third quarter of Coty's fiscal year 2020. Both parties aim to build what Coty calls a high-growth beauty brand.

Article Title: US, Israel prepare for fresh Iran strikes after midterms as Tehran threatens with ‘Father of All Bombs’
Article Text:
Iran threatens to unveil ‘Father of All Bombs’ amid reports of fresh US-Israeli strike plans

Iran threatens to unveil ‘ Father of All Bombs ’

Questions over possible use of ‘Mother of All Bombs’

US builds up military presence as diplomatic efforts continue

Pezeshkian says Iran faces a ‘super-challenge’

The United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed military strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, according to a report by The New York Times.Meanwhile, Tehran has threatened to unveil a weapon it calls the “Father of All Bombs” amid escalating tensions in West Asia.The proposed US-Israeli operation could involve a short but intensive campaign targeting Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenal.Citing US officials and others briefed on the deliberations, The New York Times reported that the two militaries had stepped up exercises, including flights over Iraq to practise strike manoeuvres.US war secretary Pete Hegseth also met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss the possibility of renewed strikes, according to the report.Some US officials believe another round of attacks could push Iran's economy to the brink and pressure Tehran into making diplomatic concessions after nearly eight months of conflict.However, it remains uncertain whether US President Donald Trump will approve a fresh operation.A White House official said the administration did not comment on military plans “that may or may not exist”, adding that Trump was keeping all options on the table to ensure Iran could not acquire nuclear weapons.Amid reports of possible renewed strikes, Iran has warned that it would respond to any fresh military action.Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said Iran was preparing to unveil a weapon described as the “Father of All Bombs”, according to statements carried by Iranian media outlets.“The United States has the ‘Mother of All Bombs.’ We will show them the ‘Father of All Bombs,’ and it will definitely be something new for them,” Mohebbi said, according to Iran's Student News Network (SNN).In separate remarks carried by Iran's Young Journalists Club news agency, Mohebbi said, “We are in the stage of preparing to unveil the ‘father of all bombs.’ This is something new for the enemy.”He did not provide details about the weapon or explain its capabilities.Mohebbi also said Iran's missile stockpile had increased 1.5 times following the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025, without providing specific figures. He claimed that missile quality, range, destructive power and accuracy had improved significantly.The IRGC spokesperson said Iran was moving towards a defence doctrine based on permanent deterrence and asymmetric warfare.“Now, we say that if a country attacks us, we will not only respond but also launch an offensive,” he said.“Our doctrine will no longer be merely offensive; it will be asymmetric. We will attack the enemy in a way that makes them feel the intensity of our response,” Mohebbi added.The Iranian threat follows reports that Trump has considered using the US GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), commonly known as the “Mother of All Bombs”, against Iran's deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility.The conventional bomb weighs approximately 9,800 kg (21,600 pounds) and is among the largest non-nuclear weapons in the US arsenal. Trump authorised its first use during his initial presidential term, when it was deployed against an Islamic State tunnel complex in Afghanistan in April 2017.However, weapons specialists have questioned whether the bomb could destroy Iran's underground nuclear facility, which is believed to be protected by layers of granite.The MOAB explodes above ground rather than functioning as a deep-penetration weapon. Military officials have also raised concerns about its delivery, as the bomb would have to be carried by a relatively slow-flying MC-130 transport aircraft that could be vulnerable to Iranian anti-aircraft fire.A separate report by CNN last week said US military planners had developed strike options that included the potential use of the MOAB against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.The report also highlighted doubts over whether the weapon could penetrate deeply enough to destroy heavily fortified underground facilities.The bomb could cause extensive destruction at the surface but might not achieve the intended military objectives against deeply buried targets.According to The New York Times, the United States is assembling a substantial military force expected to be fully in place by early November. The planned deployment includes three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces.The report said political considerations, including Trump's earlier pledge not to launch strikes against Iran before the midterm elections, could affect the timing of any operation.The US and Israel reportedly came close to launching another attack earlier this month, but Trump postponed the operation shortly before it was due to begin, despite extensive preparations and heightened alert levels among their air forces.Washington is also seeking to use the threat of renewed military action as leverage in negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme and control of the Strait of Hormuz, the report said.Iranian negotiators, however, have resisted making concessions on the nuclear issue, insisting that it be addressed later in the talks.Some US planners believe a three-day campaign could inflict enough economic damage to change Tehran's position.However, previous US-Israeli strikes between February and April drove up energy prices and inflation worldwide, affected security across West Asia and severely strained the Pentagon's supply of missile interceptors, according to the report.Iranian officials have warned that any renewed conflict could extend beyond commercial shipping and energy infrastructure to data centres and underwater internet cables.Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran's negotiator General Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, rejected the prospect of a swift end to renewed hostilities.Describing the idea that the US could conclude another round of strikes within 72 hours as a “fantasy”, Mohammadi said Iran would determine when the war would end.“Our attacks will be more fierce, creative and different,” he said. “We are determined and confident and strong planning has been put in place.”Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has described the situation as a major challenge for Tehran.Addressing the Iranian Parliament, Pezeshkian said, “The memorandum of understanding we signed was very good; we hadn't given anything. The current situation is neither good for us, nor for the region, nor for the world.”He added, “We are in a super-challenge, not a challenge. America didn't think we would stand firm despite the pressure and war, but we stood firm, and we will continue to stand firm.”Iran's representative to the United Nations also alleged, according to SNN, that Starlink had been used to identify and target locations in military attacks against Iran, adding that the country's space and scientific infrastructure had come under attack.The timing of any renewed operation could also be affected by Israel's October 27 election.Analysts believe Netanyahu could face difficulties initiating a war if he loses and becomes a caretaker prime minister.Others believe the prospect of joint US-Israeli strikes could be used to pressure political rivals into joining a unity government.With military preparations continuing and negotiations yet to produce a breakthrough, uncertainty remains over Trump's decision and the scale of Iran's potential response.
Article Summary: Iran threatens to unveil ‘Father of All Bombs’ amid reports of fresh US-Israeli strike plans. US officials believe another round of attacks could push Iran's economy to the brink and pressure Tehran into making diplomatic concessions. It remains uncertain whether US President Donald Trump will approve a fresh operation. Iran has warned that it would respond to any fresh military action.

Article Title: Beginning in 1925, Minnesota farmer John Christensen spent more than a decade transforming a cellar project into a 14,000-square-foot rock garden of castles, bridges and ponds
Article Text:
AI Representation: Minnesota farmer John Christensen began building the 14,000-square-foot Itasca Rock Garden in 1925. Image credits: Chatgpt

A retired farmer and a 1925 excavation near Albert Lea

A castle, ponds and bridges across 14,000 square feet

John Christensen’s

Itasca Rock Garden

Albert Lea, Minnesota, lies in Freeborn County’s glacial farmland, where John L. Christensen began building Itasca Rock Garden in 1925. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Rocks and geodes gathered on trips

The last work in 1938

Johnson family care from 1954 to 1985

A Kohler restoration was completed in 2022

Albert Lea is a city in Freeborn County in southern Minnesota, an area of farmland where glaciers left behind stones of many sizes and colors. This meant clearing away all the rocks on the farms yearly, which was an undertaking for the farmers. In one case in the Albert Lea community, a farmer found a different use for all these rocks. John Christensen lived outside town with his wife, Sophie. After he stopped farming, he began digging at his home and the site grew into a landscape of castles, ponds and bridges.Christensen had been farming in Minnesota for 40 years when he cleared many glacial boulders from his land, Raw Vision states and only after retirement did he realize their beauty and usefulness. In 1925, the magazine adds, he began excavating a basement for a vegetable cellar beneath their house. The SPACES Archives entry Itasca Rock Garden (Christensen Rock Garden) tells it differently. Christensen first set out to build the largest structure on the property, a rock and concrete castle big enough for several standing adults, to serve as a root and vegetable cellar.The Kohler Foundation page onstates that Christensen built a 14,000-square-foot rock garden of castles, ponds, bridges and grottos over a decade or so beginning in 1925. According to Raw Vision, the huge castle had turrets on top of it and 1925 written on its stone structure. Walkways with steps and archways ran around the ponds, while waterfalls, benches and a small castle birdhouse rounded off the project.Roadside America points out that the ponds once held fish and working fountains and Raw Vision adds that lily pads floated in them. The SPACES website describes the same landscape, with rock walls, miniatures, a circular seating area and a second, smaller castle.The Minnesota Museum of the Mississippi’s Itasca Rock Garden entry states that John Christensen and his wife often collected rocks while traveling, bringing home geodes and unusual specimens to incorporate into the garden and a second page from the same museum, titled Christiansen’s Rock Garden after an alternate spelling of the surname, repeats that detail. Sophie planted the flowerbeds and terraces, Raw Vision adds and her plantings added to the garden’s lush, storybook character.The Minnesota Museum of the Mississippi dates the most recent construction in the garden to 1938 and Christensen died in 1939. The SPACES article lists his name and the year 1939 among the garden’s decorations, a date later than the last recorded construction and the article does not say who added it. The museum goes on to state that his widow and later owners continued to maintain the garden and kept it open to the public and a postcard from 1952 shows it in use as a tourist site.Kohler Foundation says that the land was owned by the Johnson family from 1954 to 1985. After the Johnson family’s ownership ended in 1985, the site declined and was eventually foreclosed. Kohler discovered the garden in fall 2019 through descendants of the Johnson family. At the time, the foundation said that the garden was overgrown but the structure could still be seen and that the house was structurally sound.Kohler’s project was finished by 2022. Further gardening followed, including some planting in 2023 and guided tours resumed in 2024. As noted on the Roadside America website, the foundation donated the site to the Freeborn County Historical Society. An appointment is necessary for visiting; the admission fee is quoted at $5 for adults, though one should call to make sure. A Raw Vision article written in summer 2024 describes the restored garden as enchanting its keepers and visitors again almost a century after the first stone was laid, which fits the 99 years between 1925 and 2024.
Article Summary: Minnesota farmer John Christensen began building the 14,000-square-foot Itasca Rock Garden in 1925. Christensen first set out to build the largest structure on the property, a rock and concrete castle big enough for several standing adults, to serve as a root and vegetable cellar. Walkways with steps and archways ran around the ponds, while waterfalls, benches and a small castle birdhouse rounded off the project.

Article Title: In 2004, Florida researchers used 36 recycled oyster shells per reef mat, helping restore Mosquito Lagoon reefs to around 1,000 live oysters per square metre
Article Text:
Mosquito Lagoon oyster reef decline and the need for restoration

Oyster reef restoration mats use 36 recycled shells to support oyster growth

Mosquito Lagoon oyster reef restoration reaches 1,000 oysters per square metre

Plastic pollution concerns drive a shift in oyster reef restoration materials

Biodegradable oyster reef mats support growth while reducing plastic use

Florida expands oyster reef restoration with alternatives to plastic materials

In Florida’s Mosquito Lagoon, the return of oyster reefs began with a relatively simple idea: give young oysters somewhere stable to settle. In 2004, researchers started testing small mats fitted with recycled oyster shells, placing them in areas where boat traffic had damaged existing reefs. Each mat carried 36 shells, held in place by plastic ties and arranged on a mesh base. The approach was designed to recreate the structure of a natural reef in parts of the lagoon where oysters struggled to survive. According to the study published in Sustainability by MDPI titled, ‘ The Use of Non-Plastic Materials for Oyster Reef and Shoreline Restoration: Understanding What Is Needed and Where the Field Is Headed ’, over the following years, the restored areas developed into productive oyster habitat, with average densities reaching around 1,000 live oysters per square metre. The results also raised questions about the materials used to achieve that recovery.Mosquito Lagoon lies along Florida’s east coast, forming the northernmost section of the Indian River Lagoon system. Its shallow waters support coastal habitats that provide shelter for fish and invertebrates, filter water and help protect shorelines from wave action. Oyster reefs are part of that system, but large areas of the lagoon’s oyster habitat had been lost over several decades.Reportedly, between 1943 and 2009, oyster acreage in Mosquito Lagoon declined by more than 40%, according to research cited in the restoration assessment. Several pressures have contributed to oyster declines across the southeastern United States, including disease, harmful algal blooms, changes in freshwater flows and human activity along the coast. In this part of Florida, recreational boating presented a particular problem.Waves generated by passing boats could dislodge oyster clusters and push them beyond the intertidal zone, where conditions became unsuitable for their survival. The damage was especially relevant in the shallow lagoon, where natural oyster recruitment remained strong in areas away from heavily used boating channels.Researchers began developing oyster restoration mats in 2004, using a design intended to resemble the low profile of existing patch reefs. Each unit covered 0.25 square metres and consisted of industrial aquaculture mesh made from extruded polyethylene. Thirty-six recycled oyster shells were attached to each mat using plastic cable ties threaded through holes drilled near the hinge, or umbo, of each shell.The mats were positioned across the historic reef footprint at the appropriate intertidal elevation. Workers connected the individual units in a quilt-like arrangement, using cement rings and cable ties to help keep them in place. Rather than relying on loose shells that could be shifted by waves, the design provided a more stable foundation for oyster larvae to settle on and develop.Within three to eight years of deployment, the restored reefs averaged about 1,000 live oysters per square metre, according to the research cited in the assessment. Those densities met or exceeded the levels recorded on intact natural reefs in the same local environment.The findings suggested that a relatively low-profile structure could help restore oyster habitat when placed in suitable conditions. The researchers were not attempting to build a completely artificial reef from scratch. Instead, they were providing a stable base in areas where oysters had historically occurred but where disturbance had made it harder for reef structure to persist.The original mats achieved their intended purpose, but their construction relied on plastic mesh and cable ties. As concern about plastic pollution in marine environments grew, restoration practitioners began looking more closely at the materials being left in coastal waters.Microplastics have been documented across marine environments, including estuaries, and have been detected in many species. Filter-feeding animals such as oysters are of particular interest because they draw water through their bodies while feeding. The research assessment does not establish that the Mosquito Lagoon restoration mats caused increased microplastic pollution, but it describes a wider concern that adding plastic structures to marine environments could contribute to an existing problem.Removing plastic from a restoration project is not as straightforward as replacing one material with another. A substitute needs to provide enough structural support during installation and remain stable while oysters settle and grow. The Mosquito Lagoon team therefore sought to retain the basic mat design while changing the materials used to construct it. The aim was to preserve the conditions that had helped oysters establish themselves without relying on conventional plastic mesh and ties.The replacement approach used BESE-elements®, a biodegradable lattice made from potato starch, with stainless-steel wire used instead of plastic cable ties. The material was intended to provide a plastic-free alternative to the original mesh-based mats while maintaining a similar restoration method.Monitoring of the new mats in Mosquito Lagoon found that oyster recruitment was not significantly different from recruitment on the earlier plastic mats after one or two years. By the end of the second year, the biodegradable mats supported an average of 676.4 live oysters per square metre. That was a substantial population, although it was a different measure and timeframe from the average density of around 1,000 oysters per square metre recorded on the earlier restored reefs within three to eight years.The assessment also recorded relatively little physical damage. Of 500 mats deployed on reefs, eight were damaged by wave energy where protective shell bags had not been placed beyond the edges. The material did lose some mass during its first year in the water, with estimates suggesting a half-life of 4.4 to 6.7 years. That raised a longer-term question: whether the structures would remain intact long enough to support reef development under different environmental conditions.The experience in Mosquito Lagoon forms part of a broader shift in Florida, where restoration teams have been testing alternatives to plastic in oyster reefs and living shorelines. Options include natural fibres, cement-based structures, metal mesh, recycled shell and rock. Each has different practical advantages, and the most suitable choice can depend on the scale of a project and the conditions at the site.A statewide assessment of restoration practitioners found that projects using non-plastic materials were being carried out in a range of settings, from small community efforts to larger shoreline works. Many respondents reported that the materials performed as well as or better than expected, and 86% said they were willing to use non-plastic options again or recommend them to colleagues.
Article Summary: Oyster reef restoration mats use 36 recycled shells to support oyster growth. Biodegradable oyster reef mats support growth while reducing plastic use. Mosquito Lagoon team sought to retain the basic mat design while changing the materials used to construct it.

Article Title: In winter 2022, Emily Ford spent 28 days crossing Minnesota’s million-acre Boundary Waters with her dog; the expedition raised more than $5,000 and highlighted mining concerns
Article Text:
AI Representation: A skier skijors with a dog across a frozen lake in a snowy northern forest, illustrating the winter expedition Emily Ford undertook in Minnesota’s Boundary Waters in 2023. Image credits: Chatgpt

Ford’s Ice Age Trail hike and the

Friends of the Boundary Waters

sponsorship

A 28-day expedition from Crane Lake

Training at Wintergreen Lodge

Slush, wind, ice and a blizzard, then an early finish on March 11, 2022

More than $5,000 raised to send young people to the Boundary Waters

The Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness spans more than 1 million acres along Minnesota’s border with Ontario. Image credits: Wikipedia

The film

A Voice for the Wild

and the March 2023 screening in Madison

The Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness lies along Minnesota’s northern border with Ontario, a region of lakes, portages and forest that draws paddlers from across the country in summer.
