In winter, the lakes freeze and the canoe trails become snow-packed paths used by fewer people. There has been an ongoing debate about the possible copper-sulfide mining in the area near the wilderness and there have been various attempts by conservationists to keep the issue in the public eye. One such attempt was made by Emily Ford, a thru-hiker from Duluth, Minnesota, who hikes with her sled dog. She chose winter on purpose because most people think of the Boundary Waters in summer.Ford had already completed Wisconsin’s 1,200-mile Ice Age Trail in winter with her sled dog, Diggins, as the Friends of the Boundary Waters Wilderness note in the post Emily Ford to Ski Across the Boundary Waters . She was then sponsored by the group in a planned 210-mile winter journey from the westernmost point of the wilderness to Lake Superior in Grand Portage via the border route referred to as the Voyageur’s Highway. There are two listed objectives of the campaign: to raise awareness about copper sulfide mining and to promote diversity and inclusivity in the outdoors.ExplorersWeb reported that the pair would begin their journey from Crane Lake on February 11, 2022, combining skiing, snowshoeing and carrying their supplies on foot. She would pull her pulk with supplies and carry snowshoes for the portages through deep snow. The Friends of the Boundary Waters event page summarizes the journey as a 28-day winter expedition by Ford and her dog. According to Ford, she intended to bring the face of the wilderness into wintertime. The Quetico Superior Foundation article titled “Adventurer Emily Ford faced slush, wind, ice in 200-mile Boundary Waters crossing” is the source for this account of the expedition.According to the article by the foundation, Ford was trained at Wintergreen Lodge in Ely, an outfit that conducts dog sledding and winter camping. The training was done by Paul and Sue Schurke. Ford had intended to skijor behind Diggins for the whole expedition, but deep snow made that impossible. She said that Diggins is a lead dog that makes its own decisions.The article by the foundation notes that the crossing was full of freezing temperatures, slush, wind and ice, with stretches of loneliness. According to Hilleberg, the tent manufacturer, the two experienced blizzard conditions but stayed warm in their tent. The journey ended on March 11, 2022, falling short of the original destination of Grand Portage. The open water on the Pigeon River made them deviate from their route, and the two finished their journey via a ride to Grand Marais.Quetico Superior Wilderness News reported that Emily Ford raised more than $5,000 during her expedition for Friends of the Boundary Waters Wilderness to help young people from underserved backgrounds experience the Boundary Waters. In the same article, Communications Director Pete Marshall stated that Ford's story was inspiring. For Friends of the Boundary Waters Wilderness, the fundraising fits a broader goal of encouraging people to experience the wilderness. The Nelson Institute at UW-Madison notes that the Trump administration restored Twin Metals’ federal mineral leases in 2018.Those leases were canceled in January 2022, one month before Ford left Crane Lake. Less than a year after the expedition ended, on January 26, 2023, Interior Secretary Deb Haaland signed Public Land Order 7917, withdrawing approximately 225,504 acres of land in Minnesota’s Superior National Forest from new mineral and geothermal leasing for 20 years, subject to valid existing rights. Conservation advocates saw the order as an added safeguard for the Boundary Waters watershed, the institute notes.In an associated documentary of the journey named “Voice for the Wild,” Ford and Diggins travel through the wild land described by the Nelson Institute as occupying more than a million acres. The film was shown on campus at UW-Madison during March 2023, after which Ford participated in a Q&A session. After the trip, Ford spoke with the Friends and thanked them for giving voice to the Boundary Waters during wintertime.
Article Summary: The Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness lies along Minnesota’s northern border with Ontario. In winter, the lakes freeze and the canoe trails become snow- packed paths used by fewer people. There has been an ongoing debate about the possible copper-sulfide mining in the area near the wilderness. One such attempt was made by Emily Ford, a thru-hiker who hikes with her sled dog.

Article Title: From 1968 to 1977, retired North Carolina tobacco farmer Henry Warren built a 27-building miniature stone village around a large metal water tower
Article Text:
AI Representation: A miniature stone village featuring small buildings, including a church, hotel and water tower, inspired by a North Carolina tobacco farmer’s project begun in 1968. Image credits: Chatgpt

Henry Warren’s retirement from farming

A miniature waterwheel from a Hillsborough antiques shop

White flint rock blasted from the family property

A thriving North Carolina tobacco field. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

27 buildings standing at Warren’s death in 1977

The 1972 plaque and the hospital Warren was working on in 1977

Warren’s wife and daughter and the village’s upkeep

Caswell County lies along the northern edge of North Carolina’s Piedmont, in a region where tobacco was a major cash crop for generations. State Highway 86 runs through the county and passes near the unincorporated community of Prospect Hill. Hidden off the road, next to a volunteer fire station, is a grouping of little houses constructed from white rocks, quartz, bricks and cement, about as tall as a person. The little town does not have a fee or even a ticket booth for entrance; entry is free to all who visit. It was constructed by hand by a retired farmer on his property. The information provided herein deals with the man’s background, motivations, creations and post-death situation.Henry L. Warren was a Caswell County native who farmed tobacco until he retired. Our State magazine reports that he began the village in 1968 at age 75 and spent the last nine years of his life on it. The age of 75 fits a death at 84 in 1977, as Roadside America records, whereas VisitNC’s figure of 72 would make him 81 at his death and does not match that record. The Carrboro Citizen column Just Down the Road in Shangri-La describes the village as a hobby that developed over nine years and records that Warren died in 1977.The column references a story from The State magazine from 1979, titled “The Little Stone Village of Prospect Hill,” about a small village made of rocks and mortar and containing over 20 structures. Quoting from Our State, this project came about for the simple reason that farmers were accustomed to working with their hands and needed to have something to do after retirement.Our State also ties the village to a miniature waterwheel that Warren spotted at an antiques shop in Hillsborough. The magazine notes, “Some of his neighbors referred to it as White Rock Village, but he preferred the name Shangri-La.” The wheel was part of Warren’s completed village, which ABC11 describes as a collection of buildings surrounding a large metal water tower and pond.Roadside America describes how Warren quarried solid rock from his own property and worked on the village from dawn until dusk. Our State mentions white flint rock, quartz, red brick and cement as some of the materials that were used, while the steeple of the church is described as an inverted table leg painted white.According to Atlas Obscura, the stone pathway through the village is one of his inventions. Roadside America states that the total number of arrowheads embedded in the pathways is 11,000, while Atlas Obscura just mentions that there are thousands. ABC11 describes the winding pathway made of quartz, stones and arrowheads passing through tall bushes. Warren’s wife told Roadside America that as long as he had a cigarette and a Coke, he kept building.ABC11 and Roadside America both count 27 buildings in the village at the time of Warren’s death. Our State lists a church, hospital, mill, motel, movie theater, general store, jail, library, city hall and even a liquor store and Atlas Obscura adds a gym and a hotel. A bank and a gas station round out the list in Roadside America’s account and the Carrboro Citizen also places a fire station among them. The buildings stand about five feet tall, as ABC11 and VisitNC measure them. Visitors can also rest on carved thrones and feel like kings or queens of the village, a detail ABC11 highlights.In 1972, Warren engraved his motto on a stone slab, ABC11 reports, reading: “Let me live in the house by the side of the road and be a friend to man.” Roadside America notes that a sign bearing the same inscription is found at the front of his house. The same source reports that Warren died of cancer in 1977 while still at work on the village’s miniature hospital. Whether that hospital was ever finished is unclear, since WRAL and Atlas Obscura both count 27 completed structures at the time of his death.As summarized in the North Carolina Periodicals Index entry for the 1979 magazine article, his wife eventually gave free tours of the village to visitors, with children and older people coming most often. According to ABC11, currently, Warren’s daughter and her family preserve Shangri-La. In addition, the journal of visitors, which is located on a grass-covered hill above the village, contains decades of thank-you messages to the Warren family. The stone/concrete construction has contributed to the durability of the buildings, as noted by Atlas Obscura and visitors can still use the trail from the house to the village.
Article Summary: Henry L. Warren began the village in 1968 at age 75 and spent the last nine years of his life on it. The village includes a church, hospital, mill, motel, movie theater, general store, jail, library, city hall and even a liquor store. Warren’s wife told Roadside America that as long as he had a cigarette and a Coke, he kept building.

Article Title: After retiring in 1937, Oklahoma teacher Ed Galloway spent 11 years building a towering totem pole decorated with more than 200 carved figures
Article Text:
The main totem pole stands among the concrete sculptures at Ed Galloway’s Totem Pole Park. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Ed Galloway’s move to the Foyil farm

Ed Galloway’s Totem Pole Park

Restoration of Ed Galloway’s Totem Pole Park

An eleven-year build from 1937 to 1948 using 28 tons of cement

More than 200 carved figures arranged toward the four directions

Decline after Galloway’s death

Ed Galloway’s Totem Pole Park preserves a collection of concrete and stone folk-art sculptures near Route 66 in Rogers County, Oklahoma. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Mineral silicate paint applied in two layers during the restoration

Foyil is a small town in Rogers County, in northeastern Oklahoma. Ed Galloway’s Totem Pole Park sits on Oklahoma State Highway 28A, east of town and near Route 66, the historic road connecting Claremore and Tulsa. Travelers who took the turnoff found themselves on a farm that looked quite different from the surrounding fields and grassland. A group of painted concrete sculptures stands on the land, including a totem pole that towers over the surrounding trees. After his retirement to a farm that he and his wife had been cultivating for years, he undertook a project that would consume the rest of his life.The National Park Service states that Galloway was born in 1880 in Springfield, Missouri and later worked at Sand Springs Home, where he taught manual arts to orphaned boys. He purchased the property near Foyil along with his wife, Villie, in the early 1920s, as explained in the Rogers County Historical Society biography of his life. The National Park Service page on, a National Register of Historic Places entry , records that he retired to that property in 1937. The Spaces Archives notes that Galloway began creating large sculptures from tree trunks, incorporating human figures, fish and reptiles into the carvings.One of those early trunk pieces, shown in the archive photographs reproduced in the NPS paper, sits on the back of a turtle. The paper notes that Galloway later reused that turtle motif for the tall concrete pole. The paper gives the larger context behind that detail, noting that the trunk sculpture appears in an archive postcard and that the turtle base became a recurring structural idea in Galloway’s later concrete work.It also places the piece within his early wood-carving period, before he shifted to the massive concrete totem that rose over the sandstone outcrop.According to Legends of America, Galloway erected the pole in eleven years between 1937 and 1948, using 28 tons of cement, six tons of steel and 100 tons of sand and rock. According to Oklahoma Magazine, the hollow pole stands on a sandstone formation, which was found at the site of the pole and which Galloway sculpted into a turtle due to its resemblance to one. According to the NPS web page, the pole passes through nine stories, with the ground story being nine feet wide. Its height is also inconsistent. The most common height of the pole is 90 feet, as claimed by the NPS web page and the Historical Society, although preservation literature offers lower measurements, such as 78 feet.The restoration paper talks about more than two hundred hand-carved bas-relief animals and portrait busts on the pole. There are four nine-foot-high portraits at the top of the pole; these include portraits of Quanah Parker, Sitting Bull, Geronimo and Chief Joseph. The NPS page says that the sculptures usually depict birds and figures of Northwest Coast, Alaska and Plains cultures. The decorations are generally oriented towards the four cardinal directions. His source material was quite mundane. The NPS page says that Galloway used postcards and National Geographic magazines as his source material for the faces and symbols that he carved onto the wet concrete and then painted.The date of death varies between sources, with the NPS citing 1961 and the restoration paper citing 1962. The park started deteriorating after that time. According to the restoration paper, restoration work of the park started in the early 1980s under the Kansas Grassroots Art Association, while NPS cites 1988 through 1998 as the period for major restoration work.By around 1989, ownership of the park had passed to the Rogers County Historical Society, according to the society’s information on the Totem Pole Park website. Maintenance arrangements under the society continued to change into the early 1990s. The landmark was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1999. According to Legends of America, the Foyil Heritage Society is also involved in fundraising and groundskeeping.Restoration paper by the National Park Service shows that the restoration of the deteriorated paint of the poles was done through the use of mineral silicate paint. The upper part of the pole received painting in two layers, while the bottom twenty-five feet was left for a later phase of work. Silicate paint was used because it was resistant to water and algae and did not peel or fade. According to the page on the NPS website, it is the oldest and largest folk art environment in Oklahoma. There are fourteen other concrete sculptures around the main pole, including the bird gateposts, totem picnic tables and fish-shaped arch. According to the Legends of America, the eleven-sided Fiddle House is where Galloway showcased his handcrafted fiddles and furniture.
Article Summary: Ed Galloway’s Totem Pole Park preserves a collection of concrete and stone folk- art sculptures near Route 66 in Rogers County, Oklahoma. Galloway erected the pole in eleven years between 1937 and 1948, using 28 tons of cement, six tons of steel and 100 tons of sand and rock. The most common height of the pole is 90 feet, as claimed by the NPS web page and the Historical Society, although preservation literature offers lower measurements, such as 78 feet.

Article Title: In 1864, Abraham Lincoln donated a signed photograph to help Union soldiers' families; generations later, it surfaced in an old desk with a forgotten newspaper clipping and sold for $149,020 at auctio
Article Text:
The inscription confirms Lincoln donated the signed portrait to support Union soldiers’ families during the Civil War.

A photograph with a wartime purpose

Supporting Union soldiers' families

A forgotten clipping reveals its history

A rare piece of American history

Some historical treasures spend decades behind glass, carefully catalogued and admired. Others wait quietly in forgotten corners of family homes, their significance hidden until an unexpected discovery brings the past back to life. A signed photograph of Abraham Lincoln followed the latter path, surviving for generations in a Massachusetts family before emerging with an old newspaper clipping that helped establish its remarkable history. The portrait eventually sold at auction for $149,020, states an auction report by RR Auction.According to the auction report, the photograph, known as Lincoln's Penny Profile, captures the 16th US president in a right-facing profile. Measuring 2.25 by 4 inches, the carte-de-visite portrait was taken on February 9, 1864, by Anthony Berger at Mathew Brady's photographic studio in Washington.The image became one of Lincoln's most recognisable likenesses and later served as the principal photographic reference for Victor David Brenner's design of the Lincoln cent. The same photographic sitting also produced the portrait that would eventually be adapted for the five-dollar bill.This particular example carries an additional distinction: Lincoln's signature appears in ink at the bottom, while an inscription on the reverse records its original purpose, adds the description of the portrait.As per the report, in December 1864, as the American Civil War continued, Lincoln contributed six signed photographic portraits to the Soldiers' Aid Society of Westford, Massachusetts. The photographs were intended for sale at a fundraising event held on December 14, with proceeds supporting the families of local Union soldiers.Unable to provide federal funds directly to the organisation, Lincoln offered something of personal and historical value instead. The signed portraits became part of an effort to raise money for those bearing the cost of the war at home.The inscription on the reverse of the photograph confirms its connection to the Westford benefit, making it more than a presidential portrait. It is a surviving record of a wartime charitable initiative, adds the online report.As per the description, the photograph is believed to have been acquired at the fundraising event by Charles G. Sargent, a prominent Westford industrialist and civic leader. It subsequently passed to his son, Allan C. Sargent, who was known for his preservation work and involvement in historical organisations.The portrait remained within the family for roughly a century before its significance was brought back into focus. An accompanying newspaper clipping from 1924 documented Lincoln's donation of the six photographs and affirmed the authenticity of his signature, adds the report.The clipping was discovered at the back of an old frame when the photograph resurfaced in a desk, providing a valuable link between the object and its original purpose.The photograph, presented in very good to fine condition with minor signs of age, was authenticated by PSA/DNA and accompanied by documentation detailing its provenance. Its eventual sale for $149,020 reflects the appeal of an object that combines presidential history, photographic significance and a documented connection to Civil War-era philanthropy.Images Courtesy: RR Auction
Article Summary: Lincoln donated the signed portrait to support Union soldiers’ families during the Civil War. The portrait remained within the family for roughly a century before its significance was brought back into focus. An accompanying newspaper clipping from 1924 documented Lincoln's donation of the photographs and affirmed the authenticity of his signature.

Article Title: A Georgia woman said her next-door neighbour's marijuana smoke kept entering her apartment despite a no-smoking lease; after she sued, an appeals court upheld the California teachers' pension fund's i
Article Text:
Francis said the situation continued despite rules in the rental agreement prohibiting smoking (AI image)

Why a teachers' pension fund became involved

What happened in the appeals court?

Appeals court agreed with dismissal but ordered one change

A woman in Georgia who complained that marijuana smoke from her next-door neighbour was regularly entering her home, even though the building had a no-smoking policy, lost her case on Monday.Bridget Francis said the smoke made breathing difficult and affected her health. When her complaints to the apartment management failed to resolve the problem, she took legal action. However, her case against a California teachers' pension fund linked to the property business was dismissed, with an appeals court upholding that decision on Monday.According to the judgment document , Francis lived at Lakeside Vista Apartments, where she had also worked as a leasing consultant. Her problems allegedly began in October 2022, when a new tenant moved into the apartment next to hers. According to her lawsuit, the neighbour frequently smoked marijuana, and the smoke found its way into her apartment.Francis said the situation continued despite rules in the rental agreement prohibiting smoking. She claimed that she informed the companies managing the property about the neighbour's behaviour but they did not take appropriate action.She also complained that her requests for mould removal and reasonable accommodation had been ignored.After nearly two years, Francis approached the court in July 2024. She sued companies associated with the apartment complex and the California State Teachers' Retirement System, also known as CalSTRS. Her allegations included negligence, discrimination, damage to property, emotional distress and breach of contract.CalSTRS manages a public retirement system for teachers in California. Francis named it in her lawsuit because she claimed it owned Fairfield Residential, one of the companies associated with her apartment complex.She argued that the pension fund had a major ownership interest in Fairfield Residential and was actively involved in its business. In her view, this meant it should not be protected from legal action simply because it was a public organisation.The pension fund disagreed. It maintained that, as a California public agency, it had legal protection against the lawsuit. This protection, known as sovereign immunity, generally means that government bodies cannot be sued in certain circumstances unless the law permits it.CalSTRS also argued that it had not signed Francis's rental agreement and that she had not identified anything the pension fund itself had done to cause her problems.Francis submitted information about the pension fund's investment policies to support her position. However, the document did not specifically identify Fairfield Residential.The lower court accepted CalSTRS's argument and dismissed the claims against it. Francis then challenged that decision before the Georgia Court of Appeals.When the case reached the appeals court, the judges were not deciding whether Francis's neighbour had smoked marijuana or whether the smoke had affected her health. Instead, they examined whether she had shown enough to bring a lawsuit against the California pension fund.One issue was her rental agreement. Francis had accused the defendants of failing to honour its conditions, including the rules against smoking. But the judges found that CalSTRS was not a party to that agreement.There was also no evidence that anyone representing the pension fund had helped negotiate the lease or participated in Francis's email exchanges with the apartment management.This mattered because Francis had to show why the pension fund could be held responsible under the agreement, rather than simply pointing to its alleged connection with the property business.She also argued that CalSTRS's involvement in commercial activities should make it answerable in court. However, the judges found that she had not established that the pension fund had given up the legal protection available to it as a California public agency.In its October 19 ruling, the Georgia Court of Appeals agreed that Francis had not shown a legal basis for proceeding against CalSTRS.The judges considered the protections available to public agencies under California law and how those protections applied when a lawsuit was filed in another state. They concluded that the lower court had been right to dismiss the claims against the pension fund.Francis had also argued that she needed more information about CalSTRS's ownership and involvement in the apartment business. However, the appeals court found that she had not requested this information through the court process before the lower court made its decision.Although the judges agreed with the dismissal, they found one part of the earlier ruling needed correction.The lower court had dismissed the claims with prejudice, meaning Francis could not bring the same claims again. The appeals court said that was not appropriate because the case had been dismissed on the grounds that the court lacked the authority to hear the claims against CalSTRS, rather than because the allegations themselves had been examined and rejected. It therefore directed the lower court to record the dismissal as without prejudice.
Article Summary: Bridget Francis said the smoke made breathing difficult and affected her health. Her complaints to the apartment management failed to resolve the problem. She sued companies associated with the apartment complex and the California State Teachers' Retirement System, also known as CalSTRS. Her allegations included negligence, discrimination, damage to property, emotional distress and breach of contract.

Article Title: Texas tenant disputed repair charges after his family moved out of a rental home; the appeals court upheld an $880 refund from his $1,950 security deposit and awarded court costs to the landlord
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

Texas security deposit dispute began with a $1,950 deposit and a family rental agreement

Security deposit dispute escalates after Texas landlord changes property locks

The landlord's repair bill exceeded the deposit

Texas security deposit dispute reaches county court

The court orders a partial refund but rejects bad faith

Why the ruling left both parties with an incomplete victory

A Texas landlord-tenant dispute over a $1,950 security deposit ended with a partial refund for the tenant, but not the legal costs he had hoped to recover. Blake Vaughn challenged deductions made by landlord Albert Li after his mother and two brothers moved out of a rented property in Tarrant County. The disagreement involved repair bills, changed locks and allegations of an unlawful lockout. A trial court ordered Li to return $880.32 but found insufficient evidence of bad faith and awarded court costs to the landlord. As reported in Texas Second Court of Appeals by Justia US Law, in June 2026, the Second Court of Appeals upheld that judgment.The lease began on 25 March 2021, with an agreed extension allowing the occupants to remain in the property until 30 April 2022. Blake Vaughn, who paid the rent and security deposit, was not living there himself. The home was occupied by his mother and two brothers, whose move-out arrangements later became central to the disagreement with landlord Albert Li.Vaughn had paid a deposit of $1,950. Under the rental agreement, occupants were responsible for certain repairs and cleaning costs, along with damage caused by negligence or misuse. The contract also addressed smoke alarms, alterations to locks and the return of keys.Its provisions allowed the landlord to deduct qualifying expenses from the deposit, although the amount that could legitimately be charged remained disputed.The conflict emerged during the final day of the tenancy. Li said he had visited the property on the morning of 30 April and found the front door open, belongings still inside and tall weeds in the garden. He believed the family had moved out a week or two earlier. He also discovered that all four locks had been changed without his knowledge.Li said he tried contacting Vaughn and his mother about the locks but received no response. He remained at the property while waiting to see whether anyone would return for the remaining possessions. Before leaving that evening, he changed a lock so that it would work with the key previously supplied to the tenant.During the visit, Li moved some belongings from the kitchen into the backyard, explaining that he wanted to clear the interior before prospective tenants saw the property. Vaughn's mother later returned to collect her remaining items and found that she could not enter. Some of her possessions had been placed on the grass, according to her testimony.Her account differed from the landlord's description of events. Texas Second Court of Appeals by Justia US Law reported, she said she had returned on the evening of 30 April because she still needed to collect belongings, including a medical device she used daily. She also disputed the suggestion that the family had left the property unsecured, saying she did not recall leaving the door open.Text messages submitted during the proceedings showed Vaughn challenging the landlord over the removal of the belongings and the loss of access. He raised concerns about possible damage to the family's possessions and said an expensive piece of medical equipment was missing. Li eventually arranged for the remaining items to be collected on 3 May 2022. The dispute over whether the landlord's actions amounted to an unlawful lockout later became one of the issues considered by the courts.Li maintained that the property required work before it could be rented again. He said several rooms needed new carpeting, walls required filling and repainting, and a smoke detector had been removed. Other charges concerned the locks, garage door, landscaping and various fixtures.He sent Vaughn an itemised breakdown of the alleged damage, totalling $1,649.35 beyond the amount held as the security deposit. Vaughn acknowledged receiving the document and returned it with comments disputing several entries.The tenant challenged the carpet charges, saying the condition of the flooring had been an issue before the family moved in. Vaughn's mother also disputed the extent of the alleged damage. She said the walls had already contained holes in places and denied that the family had caused the carpet problems claimed by Li.Some charges were not contested in full. Vaughn did not dispute the lock replacement and labour costs, and he did not challenge a relatively small charge for the fire alarm and door stoppers. He did, however, question whether the family was responsible for other repairs and objected to landscaping expenses he believed went beyond restoring the property.Li's position on the carpet also changed during the proceedings. He acknowledged that he had inspected the home briefly on 29 April and initially considered the carpet to have been cleaned well, apart from several pink stains.The dispute had already passed through a lower court before reaching Tarrant County Court at Law No. 3. Li initially brought a small-claims action seeking approximately $1,649, while Vaughn filed several counterclaims. Vaughn won at the justice court, prompting Li to appeal the case to the county court.In the later proceedings, Li pursued claims involving breach of contract and the alleged removal of a smoke alarm. He sought actual damages, legal fees and court costs. His smoke-alarm claim relied on a provision of the Texas Property Code that can impose statutory damages when a tenant unlawfully removes or disables a smoke alarm.Vaughn brought claims of his own, including improper retention of the security deposit, retaliation and unlawful lockout. Other allegations, including defamation, libel and blackmail, were dismissed because the trial court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over them.Both parties presented evidence about the condition of the property, the deposit deductions and the events surrounding the final day of the tenancy. Their lawyers also gave evidence about their fees.The trial court ultimately allowed Li to retain $1,069.68 of the $1,950 deposit. It awarded Vaughn the remaining $880.32, finding that part of the money had been improperly withheld. The court did not find sufficient evidence that Li had acted in bad faith, however, and awarded court costs to the landlord.Vaughn appealed, challenging the refusal to award him attorney's fees and court costs, the decision to award costs to Li and the ruling against him on his statutory-lockout counterclaim. He also argued that the landlord had failed to overcome the legal presumption of bad faith associated with retaining a security deposit in certain circumstances.The appeal was heard by the Second Court of Appeals of Texas in Fort Worth. In its memorandum opinion, Justice Bassel explained that the court had found some evidence supporting relevant factual findings that Vaughn had not challenged. Those findings mattered to his arguments over the deposit, the lockout claim and litigation expenses.The decision left the original allocation of the security deposit in place. Vaughn was entitled to recover $880.32, but he did not obtain the additional relief he had sought on appeal. Li, meanwhile, was permitted to retain $1,069.68 and kept the award of court costs, despite the finding that part of the deposit had been withheld improperly.The case turned on several distinct questions: which repair expenses were justified under the lease, whether the landlord's handling of the property and access to it amounted to an unlawful lockout, and whether the evidence supported a finding of bad faith.The memorandum opinion was issued by the Second Court of Appeals of Texas in Blake Vaughn v. Albert Li, appeal number 02-25-00401-CV, from Tarrant County Court at Law No. 3. The appellate court affirmed the trial court's judgment.
Article Summary: Texas landlord-tenant dispute over a $1,950 security deposit ended with a partial refund for the tenant, but not the legal costs he had hoped to recover. Blake Vaughn challenged deductions made by landlord Albert Li after his mother and two brothers moved out of a rented property in Tarrant County. The disagreement involved repair bills, changed locks and allegations of an unlawful lockout.

Article Title: Pennsylvania began draining a lake after engineers found seepage at its dam; the $5.5 million rehabilitation project could begin in 2026 or 2027
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

What led to the early draining of High Point Lake in Pennsylvania

High Point Lake remained open for fishing and boating during drawdown

Pennsylvania planned fish health checks during High Point Lake drawdown

A $5.5 million dam project aimed to address safety concerns at High Point Lake

Pennsylvania began draining High Point Lake in Somerset County ahead of schedule after engineers found seepage at the dam’s auxiliary spillway and embankment. The full drawdown had originally been planned ahead of a dam rehabilitation project. According to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, the decision was brought forward as a safety precaution after a partial drawdown allowed engineers to inspect the dam in dry conditions and confirm structural concerns. Over the following six to eight weeks, depending on rainfall, the water level was expected to fall until only a small pool remained to help control sediment flowing into downstream waterways. Fishing and boating were to continue for as long as possible.The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission announced a full drawdown of High Point Lake in Addison Township, Somerset County, in August 2025. The process was brought forward after commission engineers found seepage at the auxiliary spillway and dam embankment during a routine inspection in July.After consulting design engineers and state dam safety officials, the commission partially lowered the lake to inspect the dam under dry conditions.The inspection confirmed structural concerns, prompting officials to recommend a full drawdown as a safety precaution. The process was intended to redirect water flows away from the auxiliary spillway ahead of a major dam rehabilitation project.Water levels at High Point Lake were expected to fall gradually over six to eight weeks, depending on local rainfall, as the drawdown began in 2025. As the process continued, the reservoir was set to shrink until only a small pool remained to help control sediment flowing into downstream waterways.The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission said the lake would remain open for fishing and boating for as long as possible during the drawdown. However, visitors were advised to use caution around muddy areas along the shoreline, lakebed, and boat launch. The drawdown was intended to address safety concerns ahead of planned rehabilitation work on the dam.During the drawdown in 2025, Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission staff planned to test the health of fish in High Point Lake. If appropriate, they would also consider moving as many fish as possible to other waterways through a fish salvage operation. The commission had lifted all fishing season restrictions, size limits, and creel limits to help reduce the fish population in the lake. These measures were in place at the time of the announcement. However, the commission had not confirmed that a fish salvage operation would take place.The $5.5 million rehabilitation project for High Point Lake’s dam was in the permitting phase in 2025. The plans included building a new dam embankment and spillway to meet dam safety standards set by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection.Construction was expected to begin in autumn 2026 or spring 2027, depending on when the final permits were issued. Once work began, the project was expected to take about 1.5 years to complete.The lake’s full drawdown was brought forward as a safety precaution after engineers identified seepage and confirmed structural concerns during an inspection.
Article Summary: Pennsylvania began draining High Point Lake in Somerset County ahead of schedule after engineers found seepage at the dam’s auxiliary spillway and embankment. The full drawdown had originally been planned ahead of a dam rehabilitation project. The decision was brought forward as a safety precaution after a partial drawdown allowed engineers to inspect the dam in dry conditions and confirm structural concerns.

Article Title: Louisiana doctors lost their bad-faith case against AIG after a $16.1 million hurricane damage appraisal; a court upheld the jury’s verdict over the insurer’s earlier $6.7 million repair dispute
Article Text:
Representative Image of a luxurious Louisiana home damaged by Hurricane Ida, featuring intricate imported décor and extensive repair work (AI-generated image)

Hurricane Ida damage sparks dispute over repair costs

Appraisal sets the loss at $16.1 million

Why the Fifth Circuit upheld the jury’s verdict

A Louisiana couple’s $16.1 million hurricane damage appraisal did not help them overturn a jury verdict in an insurance dispute. Raja and Gayathri Talluri, doctors who own a 25,000-square-foot home in Thibodaux, Louisiana, sued AIG Property Casualty over its refusal to pay their full $6.7 million repair estimate after Hurricane Ida damaged their property in August 2021. Although an appraisal later set the loss at $16,126,268, AIG paid the award in full. The couple’s remaining claim concerned whether the insurer had acted in bad faith by refusing to pay the full estimate submitted by ATA Loss Consulting. On February 10, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit upheld the jury’s verdict. The ruling highlights how insurance disputes can hinge on statutory deadlines and evidence of bad faith, even when later appraisals establish substantially higher damage estimates.The Talluris’ home featured imported décor, including flooring from Nepal and roofing tiles from Colombia. Before AIG inspected the property, the couple hired Precision Construction & Roofing to tarp the roof for $86,404. AIG’s independent adjuster, White, inspected the home on September 24, 2021. His report two days later estimated restoration costs at more than $7 million but recommended that AIG withhold payment until an engineer and building consultant assisted with the claim.Three days after the inspection, the Talluris sent a demand letter seeking policy limits, roof-tarping costs and funds to replace the roof. On October 1, AIG denied the full claim but paid $106,404 for tarping and immediate needs.After further inspections, AIG’s building consultant, J.S. Held, initially estimated repairs at $359,479.21. AIG paid $309,479.21 after deducting the policy’s $50,000 deductible. The insurer later increased its estimate and made additional payments. On November 11, 2021, the Talluris submitted an ATA Loss Consulting estimate of $6,713,922.27, alongside an engineering report from Structural Alliance. AIG disputed parts of the estimate, particularly the proposed roof replacement. The roofing dispute involved replacing Santa Fe tiles with Ludowici tiles at an additional $8,000 per roofing square, equivalent to 100 square feet. At trial, AIG adjuster Eklund compared the proposal to “going from a Camry to a Rolls Royce.” AIG also disputed claimed water intrusion in the ballroom.In February 2022, AIG invoked the policy’s appraisal process to resolve the remaining disputed damage. Each side appointed an appraiser, and the two selected an umpire after failing to agree on the loss amount. The Talluris’ appraiser, Irwin, inspected the property and prepared a valuation supported by 74 documents. On October 13, 2022, the umpire issued an award of $16,126,268.AIG paid approximately $10 million on November 9, excluding amounts already paid and additional living expenses and guaranteed rebuilding costs payable as incurred. It subsequently paid those expenses when the Talluris incurred them, satisfying the appraisal award in full. The couple sued in January 2023, alleging breach of contract and bad faith under Louisiana law. The district court granted partial summary judgment to AIG, finding that the insurer had paid all other amounts, including the appraisal award, within the required deadlines. The only issue left for trial was whether AIG acted in bad faith by refusing to pay the full ATA estimate.Before trial, the district court excluded the appraisal award and Irwin’s testimony about his valuation of the damage. The jury could still hear his observations of the property and his criticism of AIG’s estimates, as well as evidence about the appraisal process. The jury found that the Talluris had not proved AIG received satisfactory proof of loss and then failed to pay within Louisiana’s statutory 30-day period. Under the verdict form’s instructions, it did not need to decide whether AIG’s conduct was arbitrary or without probable cause.On appeal, the Talluris argued that excluding the appraisal amount and Irwin’s valuation testimony had prejudiced their case. AIG challenged whether the couple had preserved their objection to excluding the award amount. The Fifth Circuit rejected that argument, assumed without deciding that the exclusion was erroneous, and found any error harmless. The court reasoned that AIG did not know the final appraisal amount when it refused to pay the full ATA estimate months earlier. It also found Irwin’s excluded valuation cumulative of evidence the jury had already heard. Because the jury had found the first two elements of the bad-faith claim unproved, the appraisal award was unlikely to change the outcome. The three-judge panel of Circuit Judges Barksdale, Willett and Duncan affirmed the judgment in Talluri v. AIG Property Casualty, docket No. 24-30744, on appeal from the US District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, case No. 2:23-CV-377. The opinion was unpublished and is generally non-precedential under Fifth Circuit Rule 47.5.
Article Summary: A Louisiana couple’s $16.1 million hurricane damage appraisal did not help them overturn a jury verdict in an insurance dispute. Raja and Gayathri Talluri, doctors who own a 25,000-square-foot home in Thibodaux, Louisiana, sued AIG Property Casualty over its refusal to pay their full $6.7 million repair estimate. Although an appraisal later set the loss at $16,126,268, AIG paid the award in full. The ruling highlights how insurance disputes can hinge on statutory deadlines and evidence of bad faith.

Article Title: Pakistan's elite want out? Khawaja Asif flags bureaucrats' alleged exit plans to foreign shores
Article Text:
File photo: Pakistan defence minister Khwaja Asif

Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif has questioned the loyalty of senior bureaucrats, alleging that several government officials planned to settle abroad while serving the country, according to a report by Pakistan's Express Tribune.In a post on X, Asif said Pakistan had capable and honest bureaucrats, but alleged that many officials had made Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and other European countries their permanent homes over the past several years.He claimed some officers had prepared for their relocation under a deliberate plan while employed by the Pakistani government. Portugal, he said, had emerged as a destination for what he described as a bureaucratic exodus in recent years. He added that he had raised the issue on social media a few months ago.Asif said the officers whose names had surfaced in connection with the matter had held important positions and remained close to successive governments. He also alleged that an individual who facilitated permanent residency arrangements had fled after collecting substantial sums of money from several influential bureaucrats.The minister did not identify the officials or provide details to substantiate the allegations. He said troubling accounts were circulating about the matter and questioned whether senior officials who had enjoyed the privileges and respect associated with public service had remained committed to Pakistan.“Does it rise above all doubt and suspicion, or are they merely in transit?” Asif asked, questioning whether such officials viewed Pakistan as their permanent home or merely a temporary stop before settling abroad.
Article Summary: Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif has questioned the loyalty of senior bureaucrats. He alleges that several government officials planned to settle abroad while serving the country. Portugal has emerged as a destination for what he described as a bureaucratic exodus in recent years. He also alleged that an individual who facilitated permanent residency arrangements had fled.

Article Title: Pakistan army officer killed in IED blast during Balochistan operation
Article Text:
Pakistan Army major killed in Balochistan IED blast as security forces eliminate four terrorists.

A Pakistan Army major was killed in an improvised explosive device (IED) blast during a security operation in Balochistan province, while security forces killed four terrorists in a separate operation, the military said on Monday.According to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, security forces conducted operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Gwadar and Jattakabad in Kalat district on Sunday following reports of terrorist presence.During an operation in Jattakabad, the forces killed four terrorists and recovered “a large cache of arms and ammunition”, the Army said.In a separate action, security forces carried out clearance operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Pasni in Gwadar district. During the operation, 34-year-old Major Wajahat Waheed was killed in an IED attack while leading the operation.“Sanitisation operations will continue to eliminate any other terrorists found in the area,” the Army said.The military added that security forces and law enforcement agencies remained committed to eliminating foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism in the country.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif paid tribute to the security forces for killing the four terrorists and expressed grief over the death of the officer.“Major Wajahat Waheed sacrificed his life for the protection of our beloved homeland; the nation is proud of its brave son,” the prime minister said.Sharif also extended condolences to the officer's family and prayed for the elevation of his rank.Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years, with security forces continuing operations to contain the violence.A day earlier, security forces killed eight terrorists during operations in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts.(With inputs from PTI)
Article Summary: Pakistan Army major killed in Balochistan IED blast as security forces eliminate four terrorists. Major Wajahat Waheed was killed in an IED attack while leading the operation. Security forces carried out clearance operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Pasni in Gwadar district.

Article Title: US-designated LeT terrorist dies after mysteriously falling from building in Lahore
Article Text:
LeT terrorist Chaudhary Muhammed Sarwar.

NEW DELHI: US designated Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Chaudhry Mohammad Sarwar alias Abu Hashim, one of the founding members of the outfit, died after mysteriously falling from the fourth floor of Markaz Qudesia in Lahore Sunday.The incident reminded of a similar death that had occurred in 2016 when fake currency kingpin, Javed Khanani, had died after falling from an under construction building in Karachi.Sarwar was currently handling the finance wing and fundraising excercise in Punjab province under the garb of the outfit's political wing, Pakistan Markazi Muslim League. He was a close aide of both Hafiz Saeed and current deputy chief Saifullah Kasuri. Sarwar's son had also died in a road accident a few months ago.It was in 2016 tha Sarwar was designated a terrorist by the US justice department who termed himself as a senior LeT memeber in Lahore active since early 2000s, holding various leadership roles in the group. At the time, he was LeT’s emir for Lahore, a position he has held since at least January 2015."As the LeT emir of Lahore, Sarwar maintains relationships with LeT’s most senior leaders. Between 2012 and 2013, Sarwar worked with LeT’s foreign affairs chief Hafiz Abdul Rahman Makki, and in early 2013, Makki asked Sarwar for money to pay for his travel within Pakistan," the US justice department had said in its statement."Sarwar had been directly involved in LeT fundraising activities and used the formal financial system in Pakistan to raise and move funds on behalf of LeT. For example, in 2008, Sarwar led delegations of businessmen to LeT facilities for the purpose of soliciting donations for the group," it added.
Article Summary: US designated Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Chaudhry Mohammad Sarwar alias Abu Hashim died after mysteriously falling from the fourth floor of Markaz Qudesia in Lahore Sunday. Sarwar was currently handling the finance wing and fundraising excercise in Punjab province under the garb of the outfit's political wing, Pakistan Markazi Muslim League.

Article Title: Pakistani forces kill 8 militants in Balochistan, raid hideouts as abductions rise
Article Text:
The operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas (Photo: ANI).

Pakistani security forces on Sunday reportedly killed eight militants in three intelligence-led operations across districts of Balochistan province, amid rising cases of abduction in the troubled region.The operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas, according to the Inter Service Public Relations (ISPR), the media wing of the Pakistan Army.In the Panjpai area of Quetta district, terrorists trying to set up a roadblock to disrupt local traffic were "intercepted by security forces, resulting in [the] killing of five terrorists", the ISPR said in a statement.In Nushki district, security forces stormed a hideout, and two terrorists were killed in an intense exchange of fire, the army said. Around 500 kilograms of explosives were also recovered from the terrorists during that operation. In Khuzdar district, one terrorist was killed, the ISPR added.Balochistan, which borders Afghanistan, has seen a surge in abductions and attacks on civilians and securityforces in recent years, prompting the government to step up its anti-militant operations.On Saturday, unidentified armed men hijacked a bus carrying 20 trainee police officers near Mastung, on the Quetta-Karachi highway, and took them away. Their whereabouts remain unknown.On Sunday, at least 18 workers were abducted, and another was injured when unidentified armed men attacked a marble mining site in the province. The incident happened early in the morning in the remote Naal area of Khuzdar district, police said. The attackers arrived on motorcycles and other vehicles and stormed the site.According to PTI, no insurgent group or individual has claimed responsibility for the attack.The police and the provincial government have yet to confirm the incident officially, but two police officers, speaking on condition of anonymity, said 18 workers had been taken away by the attackers. PTI reported."They came on bikes and vehicles and opened fire and then rounded up the workers present at the site and abducted 18 of them before fleeing," a police officer said.Most of those abducted came from nearby villages and areas, he added, and another worker was injured in the attack.
Article Summary: Pakistani security forces reportedly kill eight militants in three intelligence- led operations across districts of Balochistan province. Operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas. On Saturday, unidentified armed men hijacked a bus carrying 20 trainee police officers.

Article Title: Pakistan’s decades of backing terror comes full circle as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa falls under emergency rule
Article Text:
The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers. In the affected districts, the constitutional distinction between judicial and executive authority has reportedly been set aside, concentrating control in unelected hands.

Decades of militant policy and blowback

Emergency rule and the erosion of elected authority

Opposition crackdown deepens rights concerns

Tribal communities face renewed uncertainty

Pakistan’s imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on October 11 has placed the province under direct federal control. It has effectively suspended the regional administration led by imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The move, which invokes Articles 232 and 234 of the Pakistani Constitution, comes amid a worsening security situation and a crackdown on opposition leaders and protesters. It has also renewed questions over Pakistan’s decades-long policy of using militant groups for strategic gains. A report by news agency ANI highlights how this policy has fuelled the violence now threatening its own territory.The emergency has extended federal control across 12 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, further weakening elected authority in a province that has long borne the consequences of Pakistan’s security policies. The move follows years of political turmoil, including Khan’s imprisonment, constitutional amendments that have weakened judicial independence, and the removal of the PTI-led provincial government.The concentration of power in unelected authorities, alongside the military’s expanding role in civilian affairs, has raised concerns over the state of democracy in Pakistan, according to a report by news agency ANI.Pakistan’s security crisis has deep roots in its long-standing use of militant groups as instruments of state policy. For more than five decades, the country has pursued strategic depth through its relationship with armed groups, while distinguishing between factions considered useful and those viewed as threats.This approach has contributed to a cycle of violence that has increasingly turned inward.As stated in the report, the state has repeatedly shifted its position towards militant organisations, including groups hostile to its own security forces. During former army chief General Qamar Javed Bajwa’s tenure, cadres of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were relocated to parts of the erstwhile Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.The consequences have proved difficult to contain. Pakistan’s struggle with militancy has exposed the risks of treating armed groups as strategic assets while assuming their violence can be directed towards selected targets.Former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton captured this danger in a widely cited remark, “one cannot rear snakes in a backyard and expect them to bite only neighbours, as they will eventually turn on their keepers”.Rather than confronting the broader implications of this policy, Pakistan has continued to differentiate between militant factions it considers acceptable and those it seeks to eliminate. The resulting security failures have placed civilians, particularly in the tribal areas, at the centre of a prolonged conflict.The imposition of emergency rule marks another stage in the concentration of power within Pakistan’s security establishment. The federal intervention has effectively displaced the PTI-led provincial administration, depriving the opposition of its remaining provincial government.The move follows Khan’s incarceration and constitutional changes that have curtailed judicial independence and shielded military leadership from accountability. Critics argue that these developments have weakened the institutions meant to limit executive and military power.The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers. In the affected districts, the constitutional distinction between judicial and executive authority has reportedly been set aside, concentrating control in unelected hands.Instead of addressing the failures behind the province’s deteriorating security situation, authorities have expanded federal and military involvement in civilian administration. The move has intensified concerns that emergency powers are being used not only to manage the security crisis but also to consolidate political control.The intervention has been accompanied by a wider crackdown on the opposition. Leaders and legislators have been detained, residences raided and political demonstrations suppressed. Protesters have faced police firing, tear gas and mass arrests.The treatment of political opponents has fuelled concerns that dissent is increasingly being treated as a security threat. The use of force against protesters has also raised questions about the government’s claim that extraordinary measures are needed to restore law and order.The crackdown comes amid concerns over restrictions on reporting from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, following earlier developments in Khyber before a blanket media ban was imposed on events in the province. Such restrictions risk limiting public scrutiny of security operations and their impact on civilians.The growing concentration of authority has therefore created a parallel crisis. While the state faces a persistent militant threat, its response has further narrowed the space for political opposition and public dissent.The latest intervention has also placed additional pressure on communities that have endured years of displacement and insecurity. Past military operations, including Zarb-e-Azb and Radd-ul-Fasad, remain associated with civilian hardship and human rights concerns.Thousands of displaced families are still awaiting return and rehabilitation. For these communities, the emergency raises fears of another period of disruption, particularly as the authorities expand their control and military involvement in civilian affairs.The consequences of Pakistan’s security policies have thus extended beyond the fight against armed groups. Tribal populations have faced displacement, civilian casualties and prolonged instability, while the failure to resolve the underlying conflict has left many vulnerable to further intervention.The emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa brings these tensions into sharper focus. A state that has long relied on militant groups to pursue strategic objectives now faces the consequences of violence within its own borders. Its response, however, has centred on expanding federal control, weakening elected authority and restricting opposition activity.Rather than resolving the crisis, the latest measures risk deepening the divide between the state and the communities it claims to protect. The removal of an elected provincial government, the concentration of power in unelected institutions and the crackdown on dissent point to a broader struggle over Pakistan’s democratic future, even as the country confronts the long-term fallout of its militant policies.
Article Summary: Emergency has extended federal control across 12 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It has effectively suspended the regional administration led by Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) It comes amid a worsening security situation and a crackdown on opposition leaders and protesters. The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers.

Article Title: Pakistan plans Moon landing by 2035, expands space cooperation with China
Article Text:
Pakistan sets 2035 Moon landing target as space programme expands, minister says (representative image)

First Pakistani astronaut to travel to China’s space station

Pakistan-China cooperation extends to lunar exploration

Space education and proposed museum

India’s space roadmap: From Gaganyaan to a Moon landing

Pakistan aims to land on the Moon by 2035 as it expands its space programme, planning minister Ahsan Iqbal said on Sunday, announcing that the country's first astronaut would embark on a space mission from China on November 25.Addressing the concluding ceremony of World Space Week 2026 in Narowal district of Punjab province, Iqbal said cooperation with China would help Pakistan advance its space exploration ambitions.Pakistan’s “first astronaut will embark on a space mission from China’s space centre on November 25, while the country aims to achieve a lunar landing by 2035,” he said, according to news agency PTI.The minister highlighted the growing role of space technology in agriculture, communications, climate monitoring, education and national security. He stressed that scientific research and space exploration were important for technological advancement.The upcoming mission is part of wider cooperation between Pakistan and China in space science and technology. According to Reuters, two Pakistani candidates, pilots Khurram Daud and Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, have been undergoing training in China, with one expected to be selected for the flight.The selected astronaut will serve as a payload specialist aboard China's Tiangong space station, conducting scientific experiments rather than operating the spacecraft, Reuters reported last month.Pakistan's space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), signed an agreement with the China Manned Space Agency in February 2025 to prepare a Pakistani astronaut for the mission, according to The Express Tribune.The two candidates had been training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Centre in Beijing, learning spacecraft systems, Mandarin and the physical demands of spaceflight.The mission is expected to last about a week. The astronaut will travel aboard a Chinese spacecraft launched from China and return to Earth with members of a Chinese crew.Pakistan does not have an independent launch vehicle or crewed spacecraft, making the mission dependent on China's space infrastructure and training facilities.Beyond the human spaceflight programme, Pakistan and China are collaborating on a Pakistani-built lunar rover planned for China's Chang'e-8 mission, expected around 2028.The rover is intended to use artificial intelligence-based stereo imaging to identify obstacles, assess distances and navigate the lunar surface autonomously, as direct real-time control from Earth would not be possible.However, Pakistan's participation in the lunar rover project is separate from its stated ambition to land on the Moon by 2035.According to Reuters, a Pakistani space agency official last month had said there was no official commitment or discussion about sending a Pakistani astronaut to the Moon under the existing partnership.Iqbal was speaking at the conclusion of World Space Week 2026, which was celebrated in Narowal for the first time in collaboration with SUPARCO. The event aimed to raise awareness among young people about space science, scientific research and modern technology.The minister also announced plans to establish Pakistan's first Space Museum at the University of Narowal to promote scientific awareness and encourage students to pursue careers in space science and technology.He said improved access to higher education was allowing students who had previously faced financial barriers to perform well academically.Iqbal congratulated the University of Narowal on securing first position at the Islamabad Science Festival, saying the achievement reflected the talent and potential of Pakistan's youth.The minister said the proposed museum would further encourage young people to explore scientific fields and pursue opportunities in space research and technology.India has also been advancing its space programme, with plans to send astronauts into orbit, establish its own space station and land an Indian on the Moon by 2040.According to the Union government’s roadmap outlined in Parliament in August, the first uncrewed Gaganyaan mission, carrying the humanoid robot Vyommitra, is targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. Two further uncrewed missions are planned before India attempts its first crewed orbital flight, targeted by 2027.India also plans to establish the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035. The proposed station will comprise five modules, with the development and launch of its first module already approved.The longer-term goal is to send an Indian astronaut to the Moon by 2040.Other planned missions include Chandrayaan-4, which is intended to demonstrate technologies for returning lunar samples to Earth, and a Venus Orbiter Mission to study the planet’s surface, subsurface and atmosphere.These projects form part of India’s broader Space Vision 2047, which aims to expand its human spaceflight capabilities and deepen its role in space exploration.
Article Summary: Pakistan's first astronaut will embark on a space mission from China on November 25. Ahsan Iqbal said cooperation with China would help Pakistan advance its space exploration ambitions. Pakistan and China are collaborating on a Pakistani-built lunar rover planned for China's Chang'e-8 mission, expected around 2028.

Article Title: Balochistan unrest: Teacher's killing sparks outrage, kin say Pak officials shielding 'death squads'
Article Text:
What are Balochistan's 'death squads'?

(With ANI inputs)

The alleged torture and killing of a teacher in Pakistan’s restive Balochistan province triggered protests by his family members and local residents, who warned that a key highway would be blockaded if authorities failed to take action.The protesters accused Pakistani forces of shielding those allegedly responsible for the death of Parvez Mazar, an Arabic teacher at Government High School Babbar Shor in Pasni, a coastal town in Balochistan’s Gwadar district, The Balochistan Post reported.According to Mazar’s relatives, he was "taken away" in front of his family on Tuesday and was found dead the following day. They claimed that members of a state-backed armed group, described as a “death squad,” took him to a private torture facility, where he was detained and killed.Protesters, including Mazar’s children, gathered outside the Pasni Press Club, demanding the immediate arrest of those responsible for his death. They demanded accountability and justice for the deceased teacher's family.The demonstrators warned that failure to address their demands would prompt them to stage a sit-in at Pasni Zero Point and block the Makran Coastal Highway, a key route connecting Gwadar with Karachi in Sindh province, Pakistan’s largest city and the country's financial and commercial hub.They demanded that state institutions take action against armed groups accused of abducting, torturing and killing civilians while allegedly operating under the protection of state agencies.Baloch rights organisations and activists use the term “death squads” to describe armed groups they allege receive support or protection from Pakistani state institutions.These groups have been accused of targeting civilians, political activists and human rights defenders in Balochistan, a province long affected by an insurgency and a security crackdown.
Article Summary: Pervez Mazar, an Arabic teacher at Government High School Babbar Shor in Pasni, a coastal town in Balochistan’s Gwadar district, was found dead the following day. His family claimed that members of a state-backed armed group, described as a “death squad,” took him to a private torture facility, where he was detained and killed.

Article Title: Strong 6.0-magnitude quake strikes Balochistan in Pakistan
Article Text:
6.0-magnitude quake strikes Balochistan in Pakistan

More details awaited

An earthquake measuring 6.0 in magnitude struck southern Pakistan near Khuzdar, Balochistan on Saturday, around 95 km south of Sūrāb, according to the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC).The German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) said the earthquake struck at a depth of 10 km (6 miles).
Article Summary: An earthquake measuring 6.0 in magnitude struck southern Pakistan near Khuzdar, Balochistan on Saturday. The German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) said the earthquake struck at a depth of 10 km (6 miles)

Article Title: Imran Khan facing Nawaz, Benazir-style exile deal? Pakistan opposition leader's big claim
Article Text:
Imran Khan

What happened in Nawaz Sharif, Benazir Bhutto's exile cases?

Achakzai demands access to prisoners, empowered parliament

Opposition challenges governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Pakistan opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai has claimed that jailed former prime minister Imran Khan is being pressured into an agreement similar to arrangements that led former premiers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto into exile, according to a report by Dawn published on Saturday.Achakzai, chairman of the Pakhtunkhwa Milli Awami Party (PkMAP) and leader of the opposition in Pakistan's National Assembly, made the claim at a news conference at the Peshawar high court on Friday. He alleged that the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) were involved in a similar political arrangement.“The same is happening today with the PML-N and PPP in government,” Achakzai said, according to Dawn.The claim comes amid political tensions surrounding Imran Khan, founder of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), who remains in prison, and opposition allegations over restrictions on political activity and the functioning of elected institutions.Achakzai was accompanied by Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) leaders Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas. He said opposition parties were in contact and that a multi-party conference would be convened soon.He also said resigning from the assemblies remained an option, adding that the opposition had submitted its demands in response to an offer of negotiations.Achakzai's remarks referred to the circumstances in which Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, two of Pakistan's most prominent former prime ministers, spent periods outside the country following political upheavals, Dawnreported.Sharif was ousted and imprisoned after a military coup led by then-army chief Pervez Musharraf. He left Pakistan in 2000 under a deal negotiated with the involvement of Saudi and Lebanese leaders.Bhutto, meanwhile, went into self-imposed exile after her Pakistan Peoples Party lost the 1997 general elections, following her dismissal by then-president Farooq Leghari. Her husband, Asif Ali Zardari, was imprisoned on corruption charges and was released in 2004.Achakzai's comparison suggests that he believes a similar arrangement could be pursued in Khan's case. However, his remarks, as reported by Dawn, did not establish that an exile agreement involving the PTI founder had been reached.During the news conference, Achakzai criticised restrictions on prisoners' access to meetings and called for changes to what he described as a "wrong amendment". He also demanded that parliament be empowered and an independent commission be established to ensure transparent elections.“Nowhere in the world is a prisoner denied meetings,” he said, according to Dawn.He argued that political disputes could not be resolved without strengthening parliament. He also expressed concern over the whereabouts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's chief minister and other lawmakers, demanding that the authorities disclose the chief minister's location.“We stand with the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The people of this province have the first right over its minerals. Regardless of political affiliation, everyone must unite for the homeland,” he said, adding that they would be safer if the country survived.Mengal, who accompanied Achakzai, criticised the government's actions in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and questioned the imposition of governor's rule on grounds of terrorism. He also alleged that elected representatives had been displaced and questioned the legitimacy of the political system.Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, also criticised the situation, saying: “You cannot run a country, yet you have occupied a province,” according to Dawn.Separately, TTAP leaders approached the Peshawar High Court on Friday, challenging the proclamation of emergency and the imposition of governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.According to Dawn, the petitioners asked the court to declare the October 11 proclamation, issued under Articles 232(1) and 234 of Pakistan's Constitution, unconstitutional and without lawful authority. They argued that the constitutional conditions required for imposing the measures had not been met or that the government had exceeded its powers.The petition also challenged the purported transfer of the provincial assembly's legislative powers to parliament, the displacement of the elected chief minister and provincial cabinet, and the establishment of the proposed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Advisory Council and Area Development Secretariat.The petitioners sought the annulment of executive orders and notifications linked to the proclamation, including the deployment of armed forces to the extent that it allegedly violated constitutional requirements.They also requested interim relief to prevent the displacement of elected institutions and restrictions on elected representatives while the court considers the case.The legal challenge adds to the opposition's broader campaign against federal intervention in the province, as Achakzai seeks to bring opposition parties together over constitutional issues, political rights and negotiations with the government.
Article Summary: Mahmood Khan Achakzai claims Imran Khan is being pressured into an agreement similar to those that led Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto into exile. He claims the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) are involved in a similar political arrangement. The opposition leader made the claim at a news conference at the Peshawar high court on Friday.

Article Title: Pakistan to chair IMF, World Bank boards in 2027; first time in over 70 years
Article Text:
The announcement was made during the plenary session of the 2026 WBG-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok (Photo: AP).

Pakistan will take over the chairmanship of the boards of governors of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group in 2027, returning to the position for the first time since 1953, the country’s ministry of economic affairs said on Friday.The announcement was made during the plenary session of the 2026 WBG-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok, where Pakistan’s minister for economic affairs Ahad Khan Cheema, who also serves as the country’s governor to the World Bank, was formally designated as the incoming chair, PTI reported.Describing the appointment as a “historic milestone”, the ministry said the role would allow Pakistan to participate in shaping global economic and development discussions and encourage constructive engagement among member countries.The annual meetings, scheduled from October 12 to 18, have brought together more than 15,000 participants representing 191 countries.The appointment comes as Pakistan continues to rely on financial assistance from the IMF through two programmes: a USD 7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and a USD 1.4 billion Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF).While the EFF is aimed at meeting the country’s balance-of-payments needs and supporting economic reforms, the RSF provides longer-term funding to help Pakistan tackle climate-related risks and improve its resilience.Pakistan could receive a further USD 1.2 billion from the IMF, subject to approval by the fund’s Executive Board. The anticipated disbursement follows an agreement reached between IMF staff and Pakistani authorities on the latest reviews of both programmes.
Article Summary: Pakistan will take over the chairmanship of the boards of governors of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group in 2027. The announcement was made during the plenary session of the 2026 WBG-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok. Pakistan continues to rely on financial assistance from the IMF through two programmes.

Article Title: Pakistan ranks lowest in South Asia on hunger index amid rising food prices
Article Text:
Pakistan's 2026 Global Hunger Index standings reveal an alarming crisis, showcasing the worst performance in South Asia amid ongoing economic challenges. (Pic Credit: ANI)

Economic crisis and food inflation worsen Pakistan’s hunger situation

Hunger reduction stalls across South Asia

Extreme weather threatens regional food production

Millions across South Asia continue to face undernourishment
