Pakistan has recorded the poorest performance in South Asia in the 2026 global hunger index (GHI), reflecting mounting food insecurity driven by economic instability, rising food prices, climate-related disasters and international conflicts, according to a report by Dawn.Titled “No Security Without Food Security”, the report was jointly prepared by German aid organisation Welthungerhilfe, the institute for international law of peace and armed conflict at Ruhr university Bochum, and swiss organisation helvetas.According to the news agency ANI, the findings indicate that progress in reducing hunger across South Asia has largely stagnated, while Pakistan and Afghanistan have experienced a deterioration in conditions since 2018.Pakistan’s economic challenges and persistent food inflation have eroded household purchasing power, making it increasingly difficult for families to access sufficient and nutritious food.The report noted that Pakistan’s undernourishment indicator had deteriorated from a low level in 2018 to a medium level. Meanwhile, child wasting has approached the threshold associated with the high category, underscoring continuing concerns over child nutrition.South Asia recorded an overall global hunger index score of 23.5, placing the region in the serious category. While the score represents an improvement from 37.5 in 2000, the report suggests that much of the progress was achieved before 2018.Over the past two decades, Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved out of the alarming hunger category. However, persistent levels of child malnutrition continue to pose a significant challenge in both countries.Child stunting has continued to decline in Pakistan, while Afghanistan has recorded a slight increase in the indicator since 2018.Child mortality rates have improved in both countries, falling from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels in the latest assessment.The report also drew attention to the growing impact of extreme weather events on agricultural production and food security across South Asia.Heavy rainfall and flooding damaged crops in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh. In Afghanistan, inadequate rainfall and unusually high temperatures disrupted the cereal-growing season in 2026.These climate-related pressures could further aggravate food shortages and prolong acute food insecurity across the region, according to Dawn.Estimates from the food and agriculture organisation (FAO) indicate that approximately 218 million people across South Asia, including Iran, experienced undernourishment between 2023 and 2025.This represents roughly one-third of the global population affected by undernourishment during the period, highlighting the scale of the region’s food security challenge.The findings underscore the need for sustained efforts to address economic vulnerabilities, improve access to nutritious food and strengthen agricultural resilience against climate-related shocks.
Article Summary: Pakistan has recorded the poorest performance in South Asia in the 2026 global hunger index (GHI) The report was prepared by German aid organisation Welthungerhilfe, the institute for international law of peace and armed conflict at Ruhr university Bochum, and swiss organisation helvetas. The findings indicate that progress in reducing hunger across South Asia has largely stagnated.

Article Title: 33 children, teacher killed as school roof collapses in Pakistan’s Peshawar
Article Text:
18 killed as school roof collapses in Pakistan's Peshawar

At least 33 students and a teacher were killed after the roof of a school collapsed in Pakistan 's Peshawar city on Thursday.Twenty students and a female teacher were killed and more than 40 people injured in the incident, officials said.Peshawar Capital City Police chief Mian Saeed said the incident occurred in Dir Colony in the city's inner area, as cited by PTI.Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson Muhammad Asim said an emergency had been declared at the facility to treat the injured.All the children killed in the incident were aged 13 or younger, Asim said. Rescue officials said 25 injured children had been taken to medical facilities.Rescue teams were clearing the debris and searching for children and school staff who might still be trapped beneath the collapsed structure.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over the loss of life and extended his condolences to the bereaved families.Building and roof collapses are common in Pakistan, largely due to poor safety standards and the use of substandard construction materials.In July, three girls aged between three and 13 were killed when part of the outer wall of a government primary school near Umerkot collapsed, burying them under the debris, as cited by Dawn.That same month, a child was killed and at least five others were injured when the roof of an under-construction private school building collapsed in Lahore’s Baghbanpura neighbourhood.In June, 14 children died after the roof of a private tuition centre collapsed in Lahore’s Kahna area. Less than two months earlier, four children were killed and 20 people injured when a classroom roof collapsed at a private school in Dera Ghazi Khan.
Article Summary: Twenty students and a female teacher were killed and more than 40 people injured in the incident. The incident occurred in Dir Colony in the city's inner area. Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over the loss of life and extended his condolences to the bereaved families.

Article Title: Pakistan regulator warns TV channels against live coverage of blasts and terror attacks
Article Text:
The regulator also stressed the need for stronger editorial oversight.

Channels told to air only verified information

Legal action for violations

Pakistan's media regulator has warned satellite television channels against broadcasting live footage of explosions, gunfire and terrorist attacks, cautioning that violations could lead to legal action.The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) issued a notification on Tuesday, reminding broadcasters of restrictions first introduced on February 20, 2023. The rules bar news, current affairs and regional-language channels from broadcasting, rebroadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.The directive comes as emergency rule has been imposed in the north-western province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, renewing debate over how the media should report security incidents while ensuring that the public receives timely and reliable information.PEMRA has instructed broadcasters to air only “verified information warranted by the relevant government departments or law enforcement agencies”.The regulator also stressed the need for stronger editorial oversight and the effective use of broadcast delays to prevent the immediate transmission of sensitive footage during security incidents.It directed television channels to establish independent editorial boards in line with applicable laws and relevant court judgments.The notification referred to the Supreme Court's judgment in Suo Motu Case No. 28 of 2018 and an Islamabad High Court order dated September 5, 2022, both concerning the prescribed procedure for broadcast delays.PEMRA warned that channels violating the directive could face legal proceedings under Sections 29A, 30 and 33 of the PEMRA Ordinance, 2002, as amended.The latest notification reiterates the regulator's existing restrictions on live coverage of security incidents, with a focus on verification, editorial checks and the use of broadcast delays.
Article Summary: Pakistan's media regulator has warned satellite television channels against broadcasting live footage of explosions, gunfire and terrorist attacks. The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) issued a notification on Tuesday. The rules bar news, current affairs and regional-language channels from broadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.

Article Title: 6 killed, several injured as passenger train derails in Pakistan's Punjab
Article Text:
Train travelling from Karachi to Peshawar derails in Pakistan (Representative image) (PTI)

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the top priority to prevent train accidents? Improving railway tracks Upgrading safety systems Regular maintenance and inspections 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

At least six people were killed and several others injured after a passenger train derailed in Pakistan's Punjab province early Tuesday, Pakistan-based Geo News reported.The Rehman Baba Express, travelling from the southern port city of Karachi to the northwestern city of Peshawar, derailed in Sher Shah, Punjab province, news agency AP reported, citing Pakistan Railways spokesperson Kaleem Akhtar.The injured were taken to Nishtar Hospital in Multan for treatment, while rescue teams continued operations at the accident site.The accident took place at around 5.15am, according to Geo News.Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed grief over the deaths in separate statements and directed authorities to ensure the best possible medical care for the injured.Train accidents are relatively common in Pakistan, where the railway system has suffered from decades of underinvestment, outdated tracks and ageing signalling systems.In 2023, 10 carriages of a passenger train derailed in southern Pakistan, killing 30 people and injuring more than 90 others.
Article Summary: Passenger train travelling from Karachi to Peshawar derails in Pakistan. At least six people killed and several others injured in Sher Shah, Punjab province. Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif express grief over the deaths.

Article Title: In Pakistan, Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu calls for early Saarc summit
Article Text:
The last Saarc summit was held in 2014 in Nepal.

Maldives and Pak sign 20 MoUs including defence, maritime cooperation

In remarks likely to ruffle feathers in India, Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu called for an early convening of the Saarc summit during his visit to Pakistan, saying Male is ready to work with other member-states to make the summit happen.The summit, which was to take place in Islamabad in 2016, was called off because of the cross-border Uri terrorist attack in J&K and the process has remained stalled since then. India maintains that regional cooperation under Saarc is possible only in an atmosphere free of terror and it’s up to Pakistan to create that environment.I believe that through this organisation, we can work together to find solutions to the challenges facing the countries of this region,” said Muizzu in Islamabad during what was the first visit by a Maldivian president to Pakistan in over a decade.“The Maldives stands ready to consult with member countries on resuming Saarc’s work. Through sustained dialogue, trust and understanding, we can strengthen cooperation within Saarc,” he said.The visit also saw the two sides signing 20 MoUs, including in areas like defence and maritime cooperation that will be of concern to India.This is not the first time though that Muizzu has called for revival of Saarc. In his independence day speech this year, Muizzu had also offered to act as a mediator between India and Pakistan to advance talks for an early leaders’ summit.The last Saarc summit was held in 2014 in Nepal. Member-states like the Maldives, Bangladesh and Nepal have from time-to-time sought revival of the summit.In its response, India has always blamed Pakistan for blocking the initiative for a connected and integrated South Asia.“India favours strong regional cooperation and has been working towards it for several decades. Everyone in South Asia is aware of which country and what activities are responsible for stymieing Saarc,” said MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, responding to media queries on Muizzu’s remarks in July.
Article Summary: Maldives and Pak sign 20 MoUs including defence, maritime cooperation. Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu called for an early convening of the Saarc summit. The summit, which was to take place in Islamabad in 2016, was called off because of the cross-border Uri terrorist attack in J&K.

Article Title: Stranded Iranian tankers, American pressure: Why Sri Lanka faces a difficult choice
Article Text:
How Iranian ships became stranded near Sri Lanka, and Colombo’s dilemma

We haven’t provided them (Iranian vessels) with anything so far, and we don’t intend to do so in the future either. ... Such supplies to vessels are usually provided by the private sector, and this is a matter for them. Sri Lankan foreign minister Vijitha Herath to local media

How US uses secondary sanctions to pressure governments

Sri Lanka’s maritime industry: What is at stake

We have informed the private sector that they should be extremely careful and act responsibly. Otherwise, they run the risk of falling foul of US sanctions Sri Lankan foreign minister Vijitha Herath

Why Sri Lanka can't defy US

What can Sri Lanka do

Limits of Sri Lanka’s strategic autonomy

Sri Lanka has announced it has no immediate plans to assist 19 Iranian oil tankers anchored in international waters off the island nation's coast, despite shortages of food, water and fuel aboard the vessels.“Sri Lanka will put its national interest first before considering any help, and the companies that supply ships are aware of possible secondary sanctions from the United States,” a foreign ministry spokesperson told reporters in Colombo on October 9.The statement came in response to a Wall Street Journal report earlier this month alleging that US officials had “pressured” Sri Lanka to prevent local shipping firms from supplying the tankers with food and fresh water.However, the foreign ministry spokesperson said the US had not communicated any threat of sanctions if Sri Lanka stepped in to help. Nevertheless, the risk of sanctions appears to be shaping Colombo's response, whether or not Washington has issued a direct warning.Sri Lanka's dilemma is not simply about whether to assist the stranded Iranian vessels, but how far it can act independently when the prospect of US secondary sanctions looms over its decisions.On February 28, the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran, triggering a war in the Middle East. Tehran retaliated with strikes against Israel and targeted American military bases across Gulf states.Iran also blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, a critical sea route, in March, prompting Washington to impose a naval blockade on Iranian ports. The US blockade was later lifted before being reinstated in July. Its resumption left dozens of Iranian vessels stranded off Sri Lanka and neighbouring nations, unable to return home.It was against this backdrop that Sri Lanka said it would prioritise its national interests before assisting the Iranian ships.But where are the ships stranded, and is Colombo legally obliged to assist them?According to Sri Lankan foreign minister Vijitha Herath, around 47 foreign ships are currently anchored off the country's coast, 19 of which are Iranian-flagged. Herath said all the vessels are stranded within Sri Lanka's Exclusive Economic Zone but outside the 12-nautical-mile limit of its territorial waters.This creates a dilemma for Sri Lanka. Article 98 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) requires states to promote effective search-and-rescue services and ships to assist people in distress at sea. However, the extent of Colombo's legal obligation to provide supplies depends on whether the sailors are in distress and the circumstances of their requests for assistance, rather than simply the vessels' location outside territorial waters.Dayan Jayatilleka, Sri Lanka's former Permanent Representative to the UN, acknowledged that Colombo was in a “difficult situation.”“We are caught in a difficult situation. It's clear to the world that we are not willingly refusing to assist, but there are reasons we have to be careful and to deliberate,” The Associated Press quoted Jayatilleka as saying.Sri Lanka's hesitation, therefore, appears to stem not from an unwillingness to help, but from the position it finds itself in: provide assistance and risk possible US action, or withhold it and leave the seafarers to their fate.Secondary sanctions are imposed by a government on third parties to maintain or intensify pressure on a primary sanctions target. Although the sanctioning government cannot directly compel foreign entities to comply with its policies, it can restrict its own companies and citizens from doing business with the third party. This puts the designated firm under severe pressure to sever its commercial ties with the primary target.Leveraging the dollar's central role in global finance, Washington uses secondary sanctions to discourage countries and foreign businesses from maintaining commercial ties with Iran or entities linked to Tehran. Although not legally bound by US sanctions in all cases, many comply to avoid losing access to the US financial system.This is where the secondary sanctions threat hits home for Sri Lanka, and the Iranian tankers are caught in the crossfire because of Operation Economic Outcast, the latest in a decades-long series of US sanctions against Iran.Announced on August 24, Operation Economic Outcast expanded the risk of secondary sanctions for foreign individuals and entities doing business with Tehran, including in the shipping sector.With so much at stake, a Sri Lankan shipping company may therefore conclude that the risks of assisting the Iranian tankers are too severe to justify providing them with services.Sri Lanka lies in the Indian Ocean, making it a key maritime hub. However, this strategic location also makes its shipping industry dependent on international trade and vulnerable to disruptions caused by geopolitical tensions and sanctions.The maritime sector, which includes shipping and other sea-related activities, has historically contributed around 2.5% of Sri Lanka's GDP. It provides full-time, direct employment to approximately 40,000–50,000 people. Around 70% of service providers are Sri Lankan-owned, while the remainder are multinational companies. Sri Lanka is also home to 130 shipping agencies.The presence of these agencies reflects Sri Lanka's integration into international shipping networks. Maintaining these connections is important if Colombo wants to expand its maritime sector and increase its contribution to the national economy. However, the threat of US secondary sanctions could complicate companies' decisions on whether to provide services to Iranian-flagged vessels, potentially putting Sri Lanka's maritime ambitions at odds with the risks of doing business with entities linked to Tehran.With its maritime industry growing, the question for Sri Lanka is whether it can assist Iranian vessels while managing the risk of US secondary sanctions.The threat of secondary sanctions is not specific to Sri Lankan companies; any non-US entity doing business with Iran could face similar risks. However, there is a significant asymmetry between Sri Lanka and larger, wealthier economies in their ability to absorb the economic consequences of a confrontation with Washington.For instance, in 2025, Sri Lankan companies exported goods worth $2,999 million to the United States, while importing $544 million worth of goods in return. While this trade surplus benefits Sri Lanka in some ways, it also highlights the asymmetry between the two countries: the US accounted for around 24% of Sri Lanka’s total exports that year, whereas Sri Lanka represents a relatively small market for American exports.Therefore, with nearly a quarter of its exports going to the US alone, Sri Lanka has a significant economic stake in maintaining access to the American market. Any disruption could affect exporters, businesses and workers who depend on it. This makes the potential costs of antagonising the Trump administration difficult for Colombo to ignore, even in the absence of a direct threat from Washington.There is also the added context of the 2022 economic crisis, Sri Lanka’s worst since its independence in 1948. The United States provided economic and humanitarian assistance during the economic crisis and reportedly supported Colombo’s efforts to secure a four-year, $3 billion IMF bailout programme, approved in March 2023.This imbalance gives Washington further leverage over Colombo, narrowing Sri Lanka’s room for manoeuvre.However, Sri Lanka has not always aligned itself with the US. In recent months, Colombo has taken decisions that diverged from Washington's preferences, reflecting its efforts to preserve strategic autonomy while balancing relations with competing powers.President Anura Kumara Dissanayake revealed on March 20 that his government had rejected a US request to allow two American combat aircraft to land at a civilian airport in southern Sri Lanka. According to Dissanayake, Washington made the request on February 26, two days before the Iran war began.Before that, on March 5, the Sri Lankan Navy rescued 206 sailors from the Iranian warship IRIS Bushehr after one of its engines malfunctioned and the vessel requested assistance. In total, Sri Lanka rescued 238 sailors, including 32 crew members from IRIS Dena, another Iranian warship that was sunk by a US Navy torpedo attack on March 4, four days after the Iran war began.Jayatilleka, the former Sri Lankan diplomat, highlighted that the stranded vessels are cargo ships, not warships, and argued that Sri Lanka has a moral obligation to render assistance.“These are cargo ships which carried oil to China from Iran. If these ships come in for some reason to our waters because they are attacked, we have a moral obligation to assist immediately,” he said.Colombo's past decisions show that it can exercise strategic autonomy. Whether it can do so again is another question.Although the Sri Lankan government has repeatedly maintained that its decisions are not influenced by US pressure, its position over the Iranian tankers raises questions about the limits of strategic autonomy in an unequal international system.Also, the fact that Colombo has acted independently in the past does not mean it can do so again without risking economic repercussions from Washington, which could be particularly damaging for a country still recovering from a severe economic crisis.Sri Lanka's final decision will therefore not only affect its relationship with the US or Iran, depending on what it does, but will also test its commitment to humanitarian principles. It will also determine how far Colombo can pursue an independent foreign policy without jeopardising its economic interests.
Article Summary: Sri Lanka has no immediate plans to assist 19 Iranian oil tankers stranded in international waters off the island nation's coast. This is despite shortages of food, water and fuel aboard the vessels. Sri Lanka's dilemma is how far it can act independently when the prospect of US secondary sanctions looms over its decisions.

Article Title: Nepal slope shifted 40cm over 48 days before deadly flood
Article Text:
ICIMOD satellite analysis detected instability nearly seven weeks before Aug 26 disaster; SMS warnings reached residents after debris flood swept through border corridor. (AFP)

A Himalayan mountain slope had shifted by up to 40cm over 48 days before it collapsed, triggering the devastating Aug 26 flood in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, a scientific assessment released on Tuesday by International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) found. The disaster killed at least 1,451 people in Nepal and left 5,745 missing, while another 43 died and 519 remained missing in China. The findings indicated that satellite monitoring could detect unstable slopes weeks before collapse, though scientists said predicting the precise timing remained difficult.The preliminary report, Understanding the Gyirong-Rasuwa Disaster of 26 August 2026, analysed Sentinel-1 satellite radar observations from July 7 to Aug 24 and recorded ground movement of up to 40cm along the satellite’s line of sight. The deformation pointed to growing instability in the rock and ice mass before its collapse.At 8.37am on Aug 26, an estimated 132 million cubic metres of rock and glacier ice broke away from the northern face of Langtang Lirung and plunged into Lhende Khola valley, sending a torrent of debris downstream. The surge reached the border corridor in approximately seven minutes, but authorities issued SMS warnings only around 9.15–9.16am — nearly 38–39 minutes after the collapse and about half an hour after the flood reached the corridor.The assessment drew on satellite imagery, seismic records, drone surveys, hydrological analysis and field investigations. Researchers identified geological weaknesses, possible damage from the 2015 Nepal earthquake, thawing permafrost, glacier changes and snow accumulation as potential contributing factors, but could not establish a single trigger.The study ruled out a conventional glacial lake outburst flood, initially suspected as the cause. Instead, a massive bedrock failure dislodged part of an overlying glacier, triggering a cascading flow of rock, ice, water and sediment through the valley.Researchers said conventional early-warning systems focused on rainfall and river levels were inadequate for detecting sudden mountain collapses capable of generating fast-moving debris floods.“This tragedy shows that some dangerous mountain slopes may exhibit measurable signs of instability before catastrophic failure,” said ICIMOD director general Pema Gyamtsho.ICIMOD scientist Qianggong Zhang said satellite-based monitoring could help identify other potentially unstable slopes for closer observation, although researchers could not reliably determine when they might collapse.The findings came two days after another major rock-ice avalanche and flood struck Nepal’s Budhi Gandaki basin on Oct 11, raising concerns about the monitoring of unstable slopes across the Himalayas.A joint scientific field investigation involving ICIMOD and Chinese researchers was scheduled to begin this week to examine the disaster site and identify other potential hazard hotspots across the Himalayan region.
Article Summary: ICIMOD satellite analysis detected instability nearly seven weeks before Aug 26 disaster. SMS warnings reached residents after debris flood swept through border corridor. Disaster killed at least 1,451 people in Nepal and left 5,745 missing, while another 43 died and 519 remained missing in China.
